<meta>This entry describes the decorative elements on a 16th-century blind-tooled pigskin binding. The transcription captures abbreviated Latin names for personified Virtues found on a decorative roll stamp on the front cover.</meta>

The front cover of this historical volume is made of light-colored, **blind-tooled leather** (likely pigskin). The design features a series of concentric rectangular frames. The outermost frame and the inner "rolls" (continuous stamped patterns) contain figurative stamps. On the left side, the roll depicts female figures representing specific virtues, each accompanied by a label. Two metal clasps remain attached to the right edge of the board, intended to keep the book's pages compressed and flat.

<note>The following text is transcribed from the blind-stamped roll on the left side of the cover, depicting the Virtues.</note>

JUSTICE
<note>original: "IVSTICI", an abbreviation for the Latin *Justitia*. In Renaissance iconography, Justice is typically shown with a sword and scales.</note>

LUCRETIA
<note>original: "LVCRES". Lucretia was a legendary Roman figure who became a widespread symbol of Chastity and moral virtue during the 16th century.</note>

PRUDENCE
<note>original: "PRVDE", an abbreviation for the Latin *Prudentia*. Prudence is one of the four cardinal virtues, often depicted holding a mirror or a serpent to represent self-knowledge and wisdom.</note>

---

<term>Blind-tooling: A decorative technique where a design is impressed into leather using heated metal stamps or rollers without the use of gold leaf, resulting in a dark, recessed image.</term>
<term>Pigskin binding: A highly durable bookbinding material made from tanned pig hide, characterized by its light color and visible hair follicles.</term>
<term>Virtues roll: A long, cylindrical tool used by bookbinders to press a repeating pattern of allegorical figures (like the Virtues) into a book cover.</term>

<summary>This page describes the symbolic decoration of a 16th-century book cover, specifically the abbreviated names of Justice, Lucretia, and Prudence stamped into the leather. These figures reflect the Renaissance interest in blending classical history with moral instruction.</summary>

->HERMETIC PHILOSOPHY<-
<note>original: "PHILOSOPHIA HERMETICA". This title refers to the esoteric tradition based on the writings attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus, blending alchemy, astrology, and spiritual transformation.</note>

<term>Hermetic Philosophy: A tradition of knowledge that seeks to understand the relationship between the divine, the cosmos, and humanity, often through the "Great Work" of alchemy.</term>
<term>Ouroboros: From the Greek for "tail-devourer"; a serpent or dragon eating its own tail, symbolizing the eternal cycle of life, death, and rebirth, and the concept that "all is one."</term>
<term>Pelican in her piety: A symbol derived from the belief that a mother pelican would peck her own breast to feed her chicks with her blood. In an alchemical context, it represents the stage of "multiplication" or the self-sacrificing nature of the transformative process.</term>
<term>Saltire: A diagonal, X-shaped cross. On this cube, it represents the intersection of the material and spiritual planes.</term>
<term>Rose: A symbol of unfolding spiritual awareness or the final achievement of the alchemical process; here, four roses appear within the quadrants of the saltire.</term>

It represents the "Hermetic Philosophy," a spiritual and proto-scientific tradition focused on the transformation of the soul and matter.</summary>

<meta>This page is the preface to a collection of alchemical texts published in 1545. The previous page served as the table of contents, listing works by Geber, Roger Bacon, and others. This preface explains the editor's rationale for publishing these "barbarous" medieval texts and defends the value of alchemy (chymeia) as a branch of natural philosophy focused on the study of metals.</meta>

# THE PREFACE OF CHRYSOGONUS
## POLYDORUS REGARDING SEVERAL
->booklets on alchemy <note>original: περὶ χυμείας (*peri chymeias*)</note> addressed to the Reader.<-

---

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a circular illustration of a landscape with classical architecture and a reclining figure.</image-desc>

<note>Chrysogonus Polydorus was the pseudonym of Andreas Osiander (1498–1552), a prominent German theologian and editor who also famously wrote the unauthorized preface to Copernicus's *De revolutionibus*.</note> SINCE I wished to release several selected booklets by the ancients concerning alchemy <note>original: περὶ χυμείας (*peri chymeias*)</note> from our library to the printers to be published—so that a greater benefit might flow from them to students of philosophy—I thought it necessary to say a few words by way of preface. For I do not doubt that many—indeed, good men, yet unskilled in the nature of things—might judge this entire branch of art to be utterly rejected and covered in silence; either because they believe it to be entirely false, or because they deem it too difficult to be investigated through great labors with an uncertain outcome. 

But I, although I was once of that same opinion, led by a desire for knowledge, have diligently examined this class of authors whenever the opportunity arose. I have gained so much knowledge of things from them that I not only congratulate myself considerably, but I also do not hesitate to recommend to others that they likewise become acquainted with them. For since all philosophy either directs speech <note>logic and rhetoric</note>, forms morals <note>ethics</note>, or investigates the secrets of nature <note>natural science</note>—and since the care of speech exists for the sake of something else, and the rule of morals is now sought from sources other than philosophy—who does not see that the part of philosophy which explains the natures and causes of things is the most excellent? 

Moreover, metals are no small portion of the nature of things, which no part of human life can do without without detriment, since they are the instruments of all craftsmen, the price of all things <note>referring to coinage</note>, and the ornaments of all dignities. I pass over the fact that they also provide medicine with an abundance of materials and supply various colors for painting; otherwise, they would be objects of great wonder for their contemplation alone. Therefore, I cannot yet decide for myself whether the knowledge of their nature is more useful or more pleasant. 

Aristotle and Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's works on minerals are largely lost; Theophrastus wrote "On Stones."</note> wrote about these things, both undoubtedly with precision (for it is fair to believe so); if their works were extant, there would perhaps be no need for students of philosophy to descend to this class of authors. But since those works are now missing, nothing else remains from which we may draw a certain and exact knowledge of them. If the impurity of the language or the uncultivated "barbarism" <note>The editor is apologizing for the non-classical, Medieval Latin style of the original texts, which Renaissance scholars often found crude.</note> in this type of writing offends anyone, they ought to consider that very few have existed in such a long age who joined remarkable knowledge of things with eloquence; nor should such a precious treasure be neglected or even cast aside because of the inconveniences of the speech. For it is worthwhile to hear the most ingenious men—taught partly by the principles of philosophy, partly by experience, and partly relying on both—discussing this art, and indeed the whole nature of metals...

<summary>In this preface, Andreas Osiander (writing as Polydorus) defends alchemy as a vital part of natural philosophy, arguing that the study of metals is essential for medicine, art, and commerce despite the "unpolished" language of medieval authors.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, natural philosophy, metallurgy, Andreas Osiander, Aristotle, Theophrastus, Renaissance science, history of chemistry</keywords>

# PREFACE

...considering, namely, what the first and proximate matter of metals is, what their efficient cause is, how they differ among themselves—whether by some substantial form or only by accidental qualities—what affinities they have, whether one can be transformed <note>original: *transformari*; this refers to the concept of transmutation</note> into another, and how they ought to be brought to the highest perfection. All of these matters, and many others of this kind, while they either investigate them or assert with great constancy and authority that they have found them long ago, provide so much light and knowledge that I for my part do not hesitate to doubt whether even Aristotle or Theophrastus <note>Aristotle and his successor Theophrastus were the primary Greek authorities on natural philosophy and mineralogy in the Renaissance.</note> could have provided as much. 

Therefore, this so notable an addition to Philosophy ought not to be neglected or despised by scholars, even if it must be scavenged here and there from a "barbarous" <note>Renaissance humanists used the term "barbarous" to describe the unpolished Latin style of medieval scholastic and scientific writers.</note> class of writers and gathered, as it were, like gold from dung. There is another not insignificant reason why you might wish to know these same authors. For after the fame of this art once filled the world, many scoundrels <note>original: *nebulones*</note> wander about everywhere professing it, though they know nothing less; they pillage the simple-minded—who are eager for both profit and this admirable art—luring them with empty hope through theft or fraud. No one will detect or more effectively convict their wickedness, fraud, and tricks than one who has penetrated into the inner shrines <note>original: *adyta*; a term for the most sacred, private parts of a temple, used here to mean the deepest secrets of alchemy.</note> of this art. For this art, without a knowledge of Philosophy (which those men cannot simulate), falls to no one; and it hands down such certain and effective tests <note>original: *examina*; trials or assays</note> for true gold and silver that no fraud—no matter how clever or hidden—can be applied that the art does not detect and utterly destroy, a matter which is also of great concern to the Commonwealth. 

Since, therefore, this class of authors enriches Philosophy and exposes forgers who are harmful to the Commonwealth, they were worthy of being known even if the art itself were nothing. Although I see no reason why we should not think it to be true. For it is plausibly asserted by men most practiced in Philosophy. And certain craftsmen, without any manifest reason for deceiving, have confirmed that they found it, swearing by all that is sacred even in published books. The emotions of their minds bear witness to them—the excitement and joy of the discovered art bursting forth within them so vehemently that it is not credible that such great simulation could be feigned by any artifice. 

It also has the testimony of history. For Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia.</note>, an author by no means to be despised, writes that the Egyptians, relying on the wealth from this art, were eager for revolution and were suppressed by Diocletian. But I shall recite his words: 

"Chemistry," <note>original Greek: Χημεία (*Chēmeia*)</note> he says, "is the preparation of gold and silver; having searched out the books of which, Diocletian burned them. Concerning the innovations attempted by the Egyptians against Diocletian: He dealt with them cruelly and bloodily, at which time he also searched out and burned the books written by the ancients concerning the chemistry of gold and silver, so that wealth might no longer accrue to the Egyptians from such an art, nor should they, trusting in their abundance of riches..."

<meta>catchword: the (original Greek: τό)</meta>

<summary>The editor defends alchemy as a legitimate branch of natural philosophy that investigates the properties and transmutation of metals, arguing that it helps distinguish true science from the fraud of "scoundrels." He cites the Byzantine encyclopedia, the Suda, to provide historical evidence of alchemy's power, noting that Emperor Diocletian once burned alchemical books to suppress Egyptian wealth.</summary>

<keywords>natural philosophy, transmutation, matter of metals, alchemy, fraud, Diocletian, Suidas, history of chemistry, gold and silver</keywords>

# TO THE READER.

aa 3

<note>original: *τοῦ λοιποῦ τοῖς ῥωμαίοις ἀνταίρειν*</note> "...thenceforth to rise up against the Romans." That is to say, **Alchemy** <note>original: *Chemia*; in this period, chemistry and alchemy were the same discipline</note> is the making of gold and silver, the books of which **Diocletian** <note>Roman Emperor (r. 284–305 AD) known for his persecutions and administrative reforms.</note> sought out and burned because the Egyptians had attempted a revolution against him. He treated them harshly and as enemies. At that time, he also sought out and burned the books about the **Alchemy** of gold and silver written by the ancients, so that the Egyptians might not henceforth gain wealth from that art, nor, relying on an abundance of money, rebel against the Romans in the future. So says the historian. Nor does he differ from other historians describing Diocletian.

The ancient **Poets**, however, suggested that this art not only existed but also how it should be practiced, through most delightful fables—perfectly rendered, yet *enigmatically* <note>original: *αἰνιγματικῶς*</note> nonetheless. For what else is the **Golden Fleece** sought from Colchis by the **Argonauts** than the investigation and shadow-sketch of this art? Concerning this, **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist.</note> says elsewhere: "The fleece was not as it is poetically reported, but was a book written on skins, containing how gold ought to be made through alchemy. Rightly, therefore, did the men of that age name it the Golden Fleece, because of the efficacy that was drawn from it." <note>original: *τὸ δὲ δέρας οὐχ' ὡς ποιητικῶς...*</note>

The Golden Fleece is not given to **Jason** unless he first undergoes certain and dangerous labors; that is, unless he first learns the **practice** <note>original: *τὴν πρᾶξιν* (praxis)</note> by exercising it with his own hands. For he who is ignorant of the **practice** possesses a book written about this art in vain. Furthermore, the dangerous voyage indicates the difficulty of finding the matter of the **Philosopher's Stone** <note>term: *lapidis philosophorum* — the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> (as they call it).

<margin>B —</margin>
Because that matter takes the place of the earth and is metallic, it is called the **Field of Mars** <note>term: *Ager martius* — Mars was the planetary/alchemical association for iron and the god of war; here it represents the "soil" of the chemical reaction.</note> after Mars, the god of metals. And because it must be purged, prepared, and perfected in fire so that it is fit to receive the "seed," it is imagined as needing to be plowed and cultivated by **fire-breathing bulls**. These bulls are the **furnaces**, which, unless they are correctly constructed and provide a continuous fire of the proper amount, either the material is spoiled, or the vessels are destroyed, and the craftsman is either struck by a noxious odor or even perishes in a fire.

Next, the **ever-watchful Dragon** is **quicksilver** <note>original: *Argentum uiuum*; mercury.</note>. The **Dragon's teeth** are **sublimated mercury** <note>term: *Mercurius sublimatus* — a white, crystalline, and highly toxic form of mercury produced by heating it until it vaporizes and reforms as crystals.</note>, because they possess the whiteness of ivory, the hardness of bone, and an incredible corrosiveness, not without poison. While it is being sublimated, it is caught in a glass vessel very similar to a helmet (which the Arabs call an **alembic** <note>term: *alembicum* — the cap or still-head used in distillation.</note>). Therefore, the Dragon’s teeth are brought to Jason in a **Helmet** so that he may scatter them in the place of seed into the Field of Mars. For the Mercury must be sublimated from that earth so many times until it is fixed within it. While this happens, it rises out of the earth like little spears, some of which are upright, some leaning, some entirely horizontal and aimed as if at the throats of enemies; they grow continuously in length so that they seem to move, taking on the appearance of a very dense army, even now most fiercely...

<meta>This page continues the preface by Andreas Osiander (writing as Chrysogonus Polydorus), specifically continuing the alchemical interpretation of the myth of Jason and the Argonauts. The previous page ended describing how Jason must face challenges to obtain the Golden Fleece.</meta>

-># PREFACE<-

...to show them fighting. Therefore, armed men are imagined to be born from the earth, who fall by mutual wounds—that is, they are finally fixed and buried in that earth. And unless the vessel were made of glass, or of a stony material <note>original: *siliceū*</note> without pores, the craftsman would be in danger from being struck by the odor <note>Alchemical fumes were often toxic; the "odor" refers to the volatile gases released during heating.</note>. Therefore **Jason**, in the works of **Ovid**, is imagined to have turned the danger away from himself and toward his enemies using a flint. Thus far the **Philosopher's Stone** <term>Philosopher's Stone: The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</term> is perfected; what remains is to lull the sleepless dragon to sleep—that is, to convert **Quicksilver** <note>original: *Argentū uiuū*; Mercury</note> through the stone's efficacy into gold or silver. When this succeeds, the victorious Jason carries away the **Golden Fleece**, which means the Craftsman has attained this most precious art. But before this happens, they sacrifice to **Hecate** in the manner described by **Orpheus**, in which sacrifice a great mystery lies hidden. Furthermore, because the same Philosopher's Stone is also said to heal human bodies, keeping them healthy and unharmed even to the end of life, **Medea** is imagined to restore Jason's father to youth. This art is also suggested by the **Garden of the Hesperides** and the fable of **Cadmus**; and Cadmus, having sought immense wealth from it, founded Egyptian **Thebes**, so that no one should wonder why this art flourished most especially in **Egypt**. These are great testimonies of this art, but far greater are those which the **Jews** assert from the Sacred Scriptures, according to the properties of the **Hebrew** language. For they say that this is also a part of their **Kabbalah** <note>A school of thought in Jewish mysticism.</note>. They claim the **Prince of Tyre**, mentioned in **Ezekiel**, practiced it; and therefore the prophet reproaches him because, through confidence in that art, he seemed to himself to be a God. For the prophet (as they say) relates that the gold and silver he held in his treasures had not been dug from the earth, nor exacted from subjects, nor snatched from enemies, but he had made it for himself, relying specifically on this art. Therefore, he is said there to be wiser than **Daniel** and to have surveyed all the secrets of nature. Likewise, they claim concerning their ancestors that the prophet **Hosea** reproached them for the abuse of this art, when he spoke to them in the person of God: "I multiplied silver for them, and they made gold for their idol." And so that you might believe this more firmly, they say that **David**, in what is for them the twelfth **Psalm**, provides a certain hidden taste of this art when he says: "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver burned in an **aludel** <note>original: *aludele*; a pear-shaped subliming pot used in alchemical laboratories</note> in the earth, or dust, refined seven times." For that is how they translate it word for word (whether rightly or otherwise, let those skilled in that language judge). And they add: "No one is so foolish that he would wish to treat silver in such a way—since it is a task of the greatest labor and utmost industry—unless, having been so treated, it became more precious." Nor would the prophet compare the word of God to such silver, but rather to pure gold, unless such silver were equal in value to gold. And this certainly agrees closely with the words of **Geber** <note>An 8th-century Arab alchemist (Jabir ibn Hayyan) whose works were fundamental to European alchemy.</note>, who says of silver: "He who knows how to further subtilize it, and after subtilization to thicken and fix it, shall join it with gold, etc." We have said these things not because we greatly desire to persuade. For if there is any solid truth here, philosophical minds will recognize and grasp it no less sluggishly than a healthy eye perceives light, or a magnet attracts iron. There are generally four kinds of writers of this art. Some follow a Method, without figures or

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page serves as a preface addressed to the reader, establishing the lineage of alchemical authorities and defining the terminology of the art. It follows the title page or introductory front matter.</meta>

->TO THE READER.<-

...with riddles, in the philosophical manner, but they conceal the matter of the stone in such a way that no one may attain what they intend unless by the gift of God. In this genre, **GEBER** <note>original: "GEBER"; likely referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential medieval alchemist</note> holds the first rank, whom certain more recent authors follow at a long distance, such as Roger Bacon—whom our own Pico della Mirandola also mentions—and many others. Some involve the entire methodically formed art in riddles, as the Poets do in the fables of Cadmus, the Hesperides, and the Argonauts, and as a certain more recent author does in a dialogue concerning the little golden book. Some, omitting the method, overshadow only the principal points with figures and riddles so that they wish to be understood only by those who have progressed so far in Philosophy that they can almost divine this art by themselves: of this kind are Hermes, Mary the Prophetess <note>An early alchemical authority, often identified as Miriam the sister of Moses</note>, Morienus, and the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba philosophorum"; a famous early Latin alchemical text</note>. A fourth kind writes about everything <note>original: "περὶ πάντων"</note>, but so simply and rustically that nothing hidden appears to be within. But in that genre, absolutely nothing sound <note>original: "οὐδὲν ὑγιές"; a Greek proverb meaning "nothing healthy" or "nothing reliable"</note> is found, but rather all things are discovered to be erroneous, false, and deceitful.

Students should begin chiefly with **GEBER**. He wrote four small works that bear witness to one another: namely, *The Investigation*, *The Invention*, *The Furnaces*, and *The Sum of the Perfect Magistery*. Certain people have corrupted this last one in various ways, dividing it into either three, five, or seven books, whereas there are only two. Having compared the copies, we have shared with our friends a version as corrected and diligently distinguished as possible; we would have also added the first book of *Roots* ascribed to him by many, but we clearly discovered it to belong to another.

It remains that we should also advise the reader concerning the name of the art, which I marvel is called "Alcumistica" by Erasmus—a barbarous and monstrous name. However, it is called by its true name by the Greeks as **CHEMISTRY** <note>original: "XHMEIA"; here meaning the art of smelting or pouring</note>, that is, the "Casting Art," because metals and things related to them—namely salts, alums, and inks—flow in the fire and are chiefly handled in this art. They are called "castings" <note>original: "χύματα"</note> from the word "to pour" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ χέω"</note>. The Arabs, however, having borrowed this name from the Greeks, prefixed the article according to their custom and called it "Alchemy." Just as they called Ptolemy’s "Greatest Composition" <note>original: "Μεγίστην"</note> the *Almagest*.

Furthermore, this art, like all others, has certain peculiar words and terms not well known to the common people; partly because they are foreign and exotic, such as *Aludel* <note>a condensing vessel</note>, *Alembic* <note>a distilling apparatus</note>, *Bearded Botus* <note>likely a crucible or specialized vessel</note>, *Alkali salt*, *Elixir*, and the like. Partly because they are used catachrestically <note>original: "κατὰ χρῆσιν"; meaning words used in a non-literal or strained way</note> or abusively, such as "To Imbibe" for "to moisten"; "To Fix" and "Fixation" for "to bring about that the matter is not destroyed or evaporated in the fire"; "To Descend" for "to melt and clarify," and many others of this kind, which will become known only through the diligent reading of the authors. Having prefaced these things, I will no longer delay the benevolent and studious reader, who (unless I am mistaken) has long been panting with a yearning mind for the inner shrines of this admirable art.

->End of the preface.<-

<summary>The author categorizes alchemical writing into four styles of obscurity and clarity, championing Geber as the primary authority. He also provides an etymological defense of the term "Alchemy" and explains technical jargon used in the laboratory.</summary>

## On the things that perfect and corrupt metallic bodies. Chapter II.

Since this science deals with the imperfect bodies of minerals, insofar as it is proper to perfect them, we have primarily considered two things regarding them: namely, Imperfection and Perfection. We base our intention upon these two. Furthermore, we compose this book concerning the things that perfect and corrupt, according to what we have investigated through our own experience, because opposites placed next to one another shine forth more clearly.

The thing that brings about perfection in minerals is the substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui"; literally "living silver," the common alchemical term for mercury</note> and sulfur mixed together in due proportion, thickened and fixed by a long and temperate decoction <term>decoction: a process of heating or "cooking" a substance in a fluid to extract its essence or change its properties</term> within the bowels of clean earth. This is produced while preserving its radical moisture—which does not corrupt, but rather leads to a solid substance that is fusible with proper ignition and extensible under the hammer <note>The author is describing the qualities of a perfect metal: it must melt when heated and be malleable enough to be hammered into sheets.</note>.

By the definition of this perfecting nature, we can more easily arrive at a knowledge of the corrupting thing. This is to be understood in the opposite sense: namely, an impure substance of quicksilver and sulfur, mixed without due proportion, or insufficiently "cooked" in the bowels of unclean earth, neither rightly thickened nor fixed. It possesses a moisture that is combustible and corrupting, and is of a thin and porous substance; or it possesses a fusion without proper ignition, or none at all, and does not sufficiently endure the hammer. I have found the first definition <insert>of perfection</insert> embedded in these two bodies: namely, in the Sun and the Moon <note>original: "Sole & Luna"; the standard alchemical ciphers for Gold and Silver</note>, according to...

And because these imperfect bodies cannot be restored to health and perfection unless the contrary is worked within them—that is, that which is manifest <note>visible or external</note> is hidden, and that which is hidden is made manifest—and since this operation or reversal is achieved through preparation, preparation must therefore be applied to them. We find that the moderns write to us of only one single Stone, complete for the White or the Red <note>The "White" refers to the work for silver, the "Red" to the work for gold</note>, which we also concede to be true. # THE PERFECTION OF GEBER

let it be congealed in a glazed dish; once congealed, let it be calcined <term>calcined: reduced to a powder through heating</term> for a day and a night in a moderate fire, and keep it thus sufficiently cleansed.

### The Cleansing of Alkali Salt
<note>original: "sal alcali" - likely potassium carbonate or sodium carbonate derived from plant ashes.</note>

Alkali salt is cleansed in the same way as common salt, and it is the "fat of glass" <note>original: "sagimen uitri" - a term used for the scum or flux used in glassmaking.</note>. First, let it be ground, and the whole dissolved in common warm water; afterwards, let it be distilled through a filter, congealed, and calcined with a slow fire.

### The Cleansing of Gem Salt
<note>original: "salis gemmæ" - rock salt or pure halite, often found in transparent crystals.</note>

First let it be ground, then let it be treated in the same manner as common salt.

### The Cleansing of Sal Ammoniac
<note>original: "salis ammoniaci" - ammonium chloride, prized by alchemists for its ability to act on metals.</note>

Let it first be ground with a preparation of cleansed common salt. Afterwards, let it be sublimed <term>sublimed: heated until it turns to vapor and solidifies again in the upper part of the vessel</term> in a tall aludel <term>aludel: a pear-shaped pot used as a condenser in sublimation</term>, until it has been totally extracted in a pure state. Afterwards, let it be dissolved upon a porphyry stone in the open air if you wish to make a "water" <note>an acid or liquid solution</note> from it, or let it be kept in its sublimed and sufficiently pure state.

### The Cleansing of Other Salts

Various other kinds of salts are still to be found, which are prepared and cleansed in the manner already described.

### The Cleansing of Alums

First, concerning ice-like alum <note>original: "alumine glaciali" - likely potassium alum, which appears as clear crystals.</note>. Many things can be prepared by means of it without any cleansing at all. However, it is cleansed in this manner: let it be placed in an alembic <term>alembic: a distilling apparatus</term>, and let all the moisture be extracted from it, which is of great value in this art. The dregs remaining in the bottom of the vessel should either be dissolved upon a stone in some damp place, or in the water extracted from it, or else be set aside.

### The Cleansing of Jamen Alum
<note>original: "aluminis Iameni" - Alum from Yemen, highly regarded in the Middle Ages for its purity.</note>

Jamen alum is prepared just like the ice-like variety, except that in this art it is of greater power.

### The Cleaning of Other Alums.

Many other alums <note>Alums are a class of astringent mineral salts, historically used in dyeing and medicine.</note> are still to be found, all of which are prepared and cleaned in the same manner as those already mentioned.

### The Cleaning of Inks.

First, concerning black ink <note>original: "atramento nigro." In this context, "atramentum" refers to vitriol or metallic sulfates used to make pigments and acids.</note>. Black ink is cleaned in this way: First, let it be dissolved in clean vinegar; afterwards, let it be distilled and coagulated. Or, let it first be placed in an alembic <note>A chemical apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distillation.</note> and the total moisture extracted. The dregs from this distillation, having been calcined <note>Reduced to powder by heat.</note> upon a porphyry stone, should be dissolved in their own water and then coagulated. Or, that water may be reserved according to the will of the craftsman.

### The Cleaning of Copperas.

Copperas, or vitriol <note>Ferrous sulfate, often called "green vitriol."</note>, is cleaned just like black ink. However, black ink possesses a greater earthiness than green ink.

### The Cleaning of Other Inks.

There are various inks, and they are found in different colors; these are cleaned as previously described.

### Concerning Glass and Boraxes.

Glass and the various types of borax <note>Fluxes used to help metals melt and join.</note>, if they have been made in the proper manner, do not require preparation.

### The Cleaning of Very Sharp Vinegar.

Vinegar, moreover—and every kind of sharp or sour liquid—is refined and purified, and its virtue or effect is improved through distillation. We have treated sufficiently of their cleaning and purification, by which means imperfect bodies <note>Refers to "base" metals like lead or tin that the alchemist seeks to transform.</note> can be prepared, purified, improved, and refined, always by the mediation of the proper fire.

# THE PERFECTION OF GEBER.

### *On the preparation and improvement of bodies in general. Chapter V.*

These bodies are prepared and purified for the purpose of the fire in this manner. For these imperfect bodies <note>In alchemy, "imperfect bodies" usually refers to base metals like lead, tin, copper, and iron, as opposed to the "perfect" gold and silver.</note> possess superfluous humidities and a combustible sulfurousness, which generates blackness within them and corrupts them. They also possess an unclean, drossy, and combustible earthiness, which is excessively coarse and hinders both penetration and fusion. These and similar things are the superfluities found in the aforementioned bodies, which have been discovered through our experience and certain, ingenious investigation. 

And because these superfluities come upon these bodies accidentally <note>original: "accidentaliter"; meaning these impurities are not part of the metal's true essence or "radical" nature.</note> and not radically, and since the stripping away of accidental properties is possible, it is necessary for us—once these aforementioned things are cleansed with artificial fire—to remove all accidental superfluities, leaving only the substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui"; literally "living silver," the alchemical term for Mercury.</note> and radical sulfur remaining. This constitutes the complete preparation of the imperfects and their perfect purification. 

The improvement, purification, and refinement of these remaining pure substances is done in many ways, according to what the elixir <term>Elixir: the "philosopher's stone" or medicinal catalyst capable of transmuting metals.</term> requires. Therefore, the method of preparation and purification in general is this: First, all superfluous and corrupt humidity in their essence, as well as the subtle and burning superfluity, must be raised up with a proportional fire; this is done by calcining <term>Calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</term>. 

Then, the total remaining corrupted substance in their "calx" <note>The powder left after heating.</note> of superfluous burning humidity and blackness must be eroded away with the aforementioned cleansed corrosives, sharp or bitter agents, until the calx is white or red—or colored according to the nature and property of the body—and clean and pure from all the previously mentioned superfluities or corruption. And these are cleansed with these corrosives by grinding, soaking, and washing. Afterward, however, the total earthiness <note>original: "terrestreitas"</note> must be destroyed or set aside...

# THE PERFECTION OF GEBER

<note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary 8th-century Islamic alchemist whose works formed the foundation of European chemistry.</note>

Ensure its good fusion by stirring the liquefied body with a perforated iron spatula. Draw off the dross <note>original: "scoria," the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</note> that forms upon it, and continue stirring the body in a steady heat until a good quantity of powder has gathered on the surface. Let that be set aside, and stir again, repeating the process until the entire body has been reduced to a very fine powder. 

Then, let that powder be sifted and placed back into the furnace. Apply a strong fire—though not so hot as to melt it—and stir it frequently. Let it remain in the fire of its calcination <note term="calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to oxidize it or remove volatile impurities">calcination</note> for a natural day <note>a 24-hour period</note>, or thereabouts, until all accidental moisture and superfluity have been destroyed, along with the combustible and corrupting sulfur. 

Afterward, let the cleaned white lime <note term="calx: the powdery metallic oxide remaining after a metal has been burned or calcined">white calx</note> be extracted. For the fire elevates and consumes every fugitive and inflammable substance from the aforementioned materials. Specifically, wash it thoroughly with cleaned common salt, alum, and with purified, very sharp vinegar. Place it in the sun or the open air, then grind, wash, and dry it again. Let this be repeated alternately in turn, until through the sharpness of the salts, alums, and vinegar, all its moisture, blackness, and impurity have been consumed, corroded, and destroyed. 

Then, add crushed glass along with the aforementioned ingredients. When the whole mixture has been made into a paste, let it be strained through a "bearded filter" <note>original: "Botum barbatum," likely a specialized alchemical vessel or filtering apparatus used for purification by descent</note> with sufficient fire. For the pure and clean body descends, while the entire earthy and dross-filled substance remains behind with the glass, salts, and alums. 

In that clean body which has descended and been restored, there is an equal and perfect proportion of clean quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui," or mercury</note> and of white, non-burning sulfur. For the fire and the corrosive agents have separated all the moisture and the fugitive, inflammable, and corrupting substance, as well as the blackness; and through the descent-vessel <note>original: "descensorium"</note>, or through the paste of salts, alums, and glass, the entire [earthy] substance has been divided.

## On the preparation of Venus,
### Chapter VIII.

Venus <note>original: "Veneris"; the alchemical name for copper</note> is also most excellently prepared by this method: Let a layer of well-cleansed common salt be placed in a crucible, and above it a plate of the metal, and above that a layer of salt, and above that a plate, and so on in turns until the vessel is full. Let it be covered, sealed with clay <note>original: "lutetur"; luted to ensure an airtight seal</note>, and placed in the calcination furnace for a natural day <note>a full 24-hour period</note>. Let it be taken down and whatever has been calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> be scraped off, and the plates replaced with new salt. And so let it be calcined by alternating turns until all the plates have been consumed or corroded through the benefit of the salt and the fire. For the salt corrodes the superfluous moisture and the combustible sulfurousness; the fire elevates the fugitive and inflammable substance in due proportion. Let that powder be ground altogether very finely and washed with vinegar until the water flowing from it lacks any blackness. From here, by alternating turns, soak it with new salt and vinegar and grind it; after the grinding, let it be replaced in the calcination furnace in an open vessel, and let it stay there for three natural days. Then let it be extracted and ground well and finely, and washed well and for a long time with vinegar until it has been cleansed and purged of all impurity. Let it be dried well in the sun, then let half as much sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride, used as a flux</note> be added to it, grinding well and for a very long time until the substance is impalpable <note>too fine to be felt as distinct grains</note>. Let it be placed in the open air or in the dung of resolution <note>a "manure bath," used by alchemists to provide steady, gentle heat for digestion</note> until whatever subtle thing is there has been dissolved, renewing the cleansed sal ammoniac if it should be necessary, until the whole becomes water. Honor this water, which water

### On the preparation of Mars.
### Chapter IX.

Mars <note>original: "Mars"; refers to Iron</note> is better prepared by this method: Let it be calcined <note>term: calcination (the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to a powder)</note>, just as Venus was, with cleansed common salt, and let it be washed with pure vinegar. Once washed, let it be dried in the Sun: when dried, let it be ground and soaked again with new salt and vinegar, and let it be placed in the same furnace for three days, as was said concerning Venus. Honor the solution—namely, the water of fixed sulfur—which marvelously increases the color of the Elixir. And let these things said concerning the preparation of the imperfect bodies <note>The "imperfect bodies" in alchemy typically refer to base metals like lead, tin, copper, and iron</note> suffice.

### On the preparation of Sol. Chapter X.

The perfect bodies <note>The "perfect bodies" refer to gold and silver</note> do not truly need preparation in regards to their perfection, since they are already perfect; however, so that they may be further refined and thinned, the following preparation should be applied to them: Take Sol <note>original: "Sol"; refers to Gold</note> beaten into thin plates, and place it layer by layer with well-prepared common salt into a calcining vessel, and set it in the furnace, calcining it well for three days, or until the whole has been finely calcined. Then let it be taken out, ground very well, washed with vinegar, and dried in the Sun. Afterward, let it be ground well with half its weight of cleansed salt ammoniac <note>term: sal ammoniac (ammonium chloride, used as a flux and to help dissolve metals)</note>, and set it to dissolve, until the whole has been dissolved into a most clear water by the benefit of the common salt and the salt ammoniac. This is the ferment for the red elixir, a precious and true spiritual body.

->On the preparation of Silver, Chapter XI.<-

Silver <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical name for silver</note> is refined and thinned, and reduced to a spiritual state <note>meaning a volatile or vaporous state</note> through the method already described. ->On the properties of the Great Elixir, Chapter XII.<-

We have now sufficiently determined the preparation of the imperfect metals and the refinement of the perfect ones, so that any discerning person may fulfill their intention regarding them. Let one therefore attend to the properties and the methods of action for the composition of the Great Elixir. For we seek to create a single substance, yet one gathered and united from many, and fixed, so that when placed upon the fire, the fire does not drive it off. It must be mixed with melted metals and liquefy with them, by means of the "penetrating substance" within it; it must be mixed by means of its "miscible substance," consolidated by its "consolidating substance," and fixed by its "fixing substance." It must not be burned by those things which do not burn gold and silver, and it should bring about consolidation and weight with proper and perfect ignition. However, do not understand "short time" to mean that it can be completed the first time in a few days or hours. Rather, it is because, compared to the work of other modern physicians <note>here meaning alchemists or practitioners of the "medicine" of metals</note> and even compared to the operation of nature itself, the Truth is reached more quickly in this way. Whence the philosopher said:
> Medicine is that which anticipates a long space of time.
Therefore I tell you to endure with patience, because perhaps it lingers; and indeed, haste is of the devil.

Therefore, he who does not possess patience should stay his hand from the work, because a hasty belief will only hinder him. To these, a third must be added to shorten the work: that is, the "perfect body" <note>Usually referring to gold or silver</note> in a thinned or refined state.

### Epilogue and Conclusion of the Work.
### Chapter XIII.

From the premises already stated, those things in which the truth is near are now evident. Those who complete the work itself do so through our true investigation, by which we are certain; for through manifest experience, we have considered all the words to be true which have been written by us alone in our volumes, according to what we have seen through experiment and reason as reported in these books. Indeed, those things which we have extracted with our own fingers through our experience, seen with our eyes, and touched with our hands, we have written in the *Summary of Our Perfect Mastery*. Therefore, let the wise craftsman study our volumes, gathering together our scattered intentions which we have set forth in diverse places—lest they be made public to the wicked or the ignorant—and let him prove what he has gathered until, through study, he reaches full knowledge.

And through experimenting with the persistence of ingenious labor, he shall arrive at the total [knowledge]. Through this consideration, we have reached the perfect and complete end of this science, which we have written perfectly and completely in our books. Study, therefore, in them, and you will find the whole of our science, which we have abridged from the books of the ancients.

->The division of obstacles.<-
->Chapter III.<-

There are, therefore, two general obstacles occurring in this work: namely, natural inability, and the lack of necessary funds, or occupations and labors. However, we say that natural inability is manifold. Specifically, on the part of the craftsman's physical organs <note>referring to the bodily senses and physical health</note>, and on the part of the soul. On the part of the craftsman's organs, it is manifold: either because the organ is weak, or entirely corrupted. Finally, from the inabilities of the soul, it is manifold: either because the soul is perverse in its organs, possessing no rectitude or reason in itself on account of the organs—such as the soul of an insane person or a fool—or because it is "fantastic" <note>original: "fantastica"; here meaning prone to overactive imagination or unstable mental images</note>, unduly and easily receptive to the contrary of forms, suddenly stretching from one piece of knowledge to its opposite, and likewise from one desire to its opposite.

# THE SUM OF PERFECTION BY GEBER

### *On the impediments to this work, regarding the body of the craftsman. Chapter 4.*

We have already defined for you the impediments to this work in a general sense. Now, however, we shall address you in this chapter with more specific speech, and we will describe all those impediments to you more openly, fully, and in order. We say, therefore: that if anyone does not have his organs complete, he will not be able to reach the completion of this work by himself—as if he were blind, or missing his extremities—since they are not assisted by the limbs through which this art is perfected, serving as the ministers of nature. Furthermore, if the body of the craftsman is weak and sickly, such as the bodies of those suffering from fevers, or lepers whose limbs are failing, or those laboring in the final stages of life, or men of a decrepit old age, he will not reach the completion of the art. Therefore, by these natural incapacities of the body, the craftsman is hindered in his intention.

### *On the impediments regarding the soul of the craftsman. Chapter 5.*

We have set before you one chapter in which we described, in absolute and manifest speech, the impediments depending on the body of the craftsman. It remains for us to describe briefly the impediments on the part of the soul <note>original: "animæ"; in this context, it refers to the intellect, spirit, and psychological temperament</note> itself, which greatly hinder the completion of this work. We say, therefore, that he who does not possess a natural genius <note>original: "ingenium naturale"; the innate talent or intellectual capacity</note>, and a soul subtly investigating natural principles, the foundations of nature, and the crafts which are able to follow nature in the properties of her action, will not find the true root of this most precious science. Just as there are many who are stiff-necked <note>original: "duram habent ceruicem"; an idiom for being stubborn or inflexible in thought</note>,

# THE SUM OF PERFECTION BY GEBER. 21

We have reduced to two chapters all the impediments that delay the goal of this art, which arise from radical principles according to the nature of the materials of this most precious business. It is now necessary for us to finally recount the impediments that come from the outside, arising from the fortunes and accidents of chance, by which this most glorious work is hindered. We see, therefore, certain astute and ingenious men, by no means ignorant of the works of nature, who follow her principles and works wherever possible; men whose investigation is not based on fantasy in all things governed by the movements and actions of nature beneath the lunar circle <note>The "sublunary" sphere, referring to the Earthly realm where things are subject to change and decay, as opposed to the unchanging heavens.</note>. Yet these men, oppressed by extreme poverty and a lack of resources, are forced to set aside this most excellent Mastery <note>original: "Magisterium" – the Great Work or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note>. There are also many others besides those just mentioned who are curious but held back by the various cares and anxieties of this world, occupying themselves entirely with secular business, from whom this precious science of ours utterly flees. Now, therefore, it is sufficiently clear to you from the preceding chapters what the impediments are that distract one from this art.

This is because what is not attained through natural wit is supplemented by doctrine to remedy the defect. They are ignorant, and they wastefully destroy their entire treasure; when they have come close to the end of their resources, they have nothing left with which to work. Thus, such men are buried in a double sorrow: both because they have squandered their money on useless things, and because they lose the most noble knowledge, which they might have otherwise discovered. For it is not necessary to consume all your goods, since at a low price (if you are not ignorant of the principles of the art, and if you correctly understand those things we have handed down to you) you will arrive at the completion of the <term>Mastery</term> <note>The "Magisterium" or Mastery refers to the successful creation of the Philosopher's Stone or the completion of the alchemical Great Work.</note>. If, therefore, you lose your money by not attending to our warnings, which we have written for you in this book in an open and manifest way, do not unfairly criticize us, nor heap blasphemies upon us, but impute it to your own ignorance and presumption.

Therefore, this science is not well-suited to a poor or needy man; rather, it is his enemy and adversary. Nor should he strive to find a <term>sophistical</term> <note>In alchemy, "sophistic" refers to fraudulent or "fake" alchemy—methods that produce something looking like gold but lacking its true essence.</note> goal for the work, but let him be intent on the completion alone. For our art is kept in the Divine power; He bestows it upon whom He wills and withdraws it, He who is glorious, sublime, and filled with all justice and goodness. For perhaps, as a punishment for a sophistical work, He might deny the art to you, and cruelly thrust you into the bypass of error, and from error into unhappiness and perpetual misery.

For he is most miserable and unhappy to whom God, after the end of his work and labor, always denies the sight of the truth; because he always concludes and ends the span of his life in error. Such a man, established in perpetual labor and besieged by every misfortune and unhappiness, loses all the consolation, joy, and delight of this world, and consumes his life in sorrow without profit.

Let the practitioner likewise study, when he is engaged in the work, to seal in his mind all the signs that appear in every <term>decoction</term> <note>Decoction: the process of heating or boiling a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or change its state.</note>, and to inquire into their causes. These, therefore, are the things necessary for an artist suitable for our art. If, however, he lacks any of those things we have described, let him not cling to this art.

## FIRST BOOK, IN WHICH ARE

->A general division of the things to be discussed. Chapter VIII.<-

Since in the summary of this our little book we have already set before you all the obstacles to this work, and have given you instruction sufficient for adhering to this art <note>The "art" referred to throughout is Alchemy, the transformation of base metals into noble ones</note>, it is now expedient, according to the intention of our proposal, to dispute against the sophists <note>original: "sophisticos" - those using clever but false arguments</note> and the ignorant. First, we shall set forth their own arguments, according to what we promised from the beginning that we would determine. Finally, we shall indeed destroy them all, so that by clear demonstration it may be made manifest to the wise that those arguments contain nothing of the truth.

->Various arguments of those who simply<-
->deny the art. Chapter IX.<-

There are, moreover, various people who deny and destroy it. For some do so simply, while others do so based on the statements made by those who suppose the art to exist. There are some asserting that the art simply does not exist, corroborating their opinion sophistically in such a manner; for they say: The species and diversities of things are distinct because the proportions of the elements <term>elements: the four classical building blocks—Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</term> to one another in their mixture are diverse and distinct. For an ass is different from a man in species because it had a much different proportion of elements in its composition; and so it is to be brought forward in the other diversities of things, and therefore also in minerals. Therefore, if the proportion of the things to be mixed—by which the form and perfection of a thing is obtained—is unknown, how can one form both the mixture and the thing to be mixed?

For you are scarcely able to reach the goal of a hundred years of life. If, however, it is answered in this way: "That which nature cannot perfect except in a vast space of time, we fulfill in a short time through our craft; for craft completes the defect of nature in many things." To this we say again, that this is impossible, especially in metals, since they are composed of most subtle vapors <note>original: "fumi subtilissimi"</note> which require a tempered "cooking" <term>decoction: the process of maturing or ripening through steady heat</term> so that their own moisture may be thickened within them according to a proper balance, and not flee from them, leaving them deprived of all moisture—the very thing by which they maintain their cohesion and malleability. 

If, therefore, through your craft you wish to shorten the time of nature's cooking in minerals and metallic bodies, it will be necessary to do this through an excess of heat; but this heat will not balance the substance, but rather, by dissolving the moisture, it will scatter and destroy it. For only a tempered heat thickens moisture and perfects a mixture, not an excessive fire. Similarly, being and perfection are granted by the stars, as the primary perfectors and movers of the nature of generation and corruption toward being and non-being.

We say, therefore, that the principles upon which nature founds its action are of the hardest and strongest composition; and these are sulfur and quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum," literally "living silver," the historical term for mercury</note>, as certain philosophers say. Therefore, because they are of the hardest and strongest composition, they are also most difficult to break down <note>original: "resolutionis," referring to the chemical process of dissolving or decomposing a substance</note>. However, so that their thickening <note>original: "inspissatio"</note> and hardening may occur in such a way that they can be hammered and stretched by the force of a mallet without shattering, it happens only because the viscous moisture in their mutual mixture is preserved through successive cooking <note>original: "decoctionem," a process of heating a substance in liquid</note> within the ore.

But we hand down to you a general rule, dearest son: that there is no thickening of any moisture unless there is first an evaporation of the most subtle parts of that moisture, and a preservation of the thicker parts. This occurs if the moisture in the mixture overcomes the dryness, and if there is a true mixing of the dry and the moist, so that the moisture is tempered by the dry, and the dry by the moist. Thus, this substance becomes one in its parts, uniform <note>original: "homœomera," a term from Aristotelian physics meaning a substance that is the same throughout, like gold or water</note>, tempered between hard and soft, and capable of being stretched when struck.

But this does not happen except through the long-lasting mixing of viscous moisture and subtle earthiness down to the smallest particles, until that same moisture becomes one with the dry, and the dry with the moist. And the breakdown of this kind of subtle vapor does not happen suddenly; rather, it happens gradually over thousands of years. This is because the substance of nature's principles is uniform; therefore, if the breakdown of the superfluous moisture happened suddenly, since the moisture does not differ from the dry due to the strong mixture they possess, the moisture would certainly break down along with the dry. Consequently, the whole thing would vanish into smoke, and the moisture could not be separated from the dry during the breakdown because of the strong union they have with one another.

We see clear evidence of this in the sublimation <term>Sublimation: the alchemical process of heating a solid until it turns into a vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</term> of spirits; because when a sudden breakdown occurs in them through sublimation, the moisture is not separated from the dry, nor the dry from the moisture,

### Refutation of the arguments of those who simply deny the art. Chapter XI.

If they should say, therefore, that we are ignorant of the proportion of the elements, the manner of their mixing with one another, the balancing of the heat that thickens metals, and many other causes and accidents following the natural actions; we certainly grant this to them. But they do not destroy our divine science because of this, for we neither wish to know those things, nor can we, nor can they be applied to our work. Instead, we assume another principle for this task, and another method for the generation of metals, in which we are able to follow nature. If they say that even the philosophers and the Princes of this world have desired this science and have not found it: we respond that they lie. For it is certain that some Princes (though few) and especially the ancients and the wise men found in our own time, have already investigated this science through their own industry; but they did not wish to hand it down to such people <note>The "sophists" or the unworthy.</note> either by word of mouth or in writings.

Perfection consists more in proportion and composition than in anything else. For indeed, species is changed into species in this way: when an individual of one species is transformed into that of another. For we see a worm, both naturally and through natural artifice, turn into a fly, which differs from it in species; and a strangled calf turns into bees <note>a reference to the ancient belief in 'bugonia' or spontaneous generation</note>, and wheat into tares, and a strangled dog into worms through the boiling heat of putrefaction.

We assign the cause of this to be that it has a strong composition, and therefore it has a more difficult resolution <term>dissolution</term> <note>The breaking down of a substance into its primary components</note>, and thus it is destroyed with difficulty. And this is what makes them opine that its construction is impossible, because they are ignorant of artificial destruction according to the course of nature. They perhaps attempted it because it is of a strong composition, but how strong that composition truly is, they did not attempt to discover.

### *The diverse opinions of those who suppose the art to exist. Chapter XII.*

Therefore, among those who suppose this art to exist, we find them to be manifold in their differing intentions. Some place it in spirits <note>In alchemy, "spirits" usually refer to volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, arsenic, and sal ammoniac.</note>. Others, however, in bodies <note>Metals in their solid state.</note>. Others in salts and alums, nitres and boraxes. Still others affirm that this art and mastery is found in all vegetable things. Among all these, some have judged and handed down this divine mastery to posterity well in part and poorly in part, while others have done so poorly in its entirety. It happened that we collected the truth from the multiplicities of their errors through difficult and laborious careful conjecture, long and tedious experience, and the outlay of great expense. Their error often campaigned against the disposition and reasoning of our mind, and nearly brought us to despair. May they be cursed forever, therefore, because they left behind blasphemies and a curse to posterity; through their error, they persuaded those studying philosophy <note>original: "philosophantes"</note> of falsehoods; they left behind not the truth, but rather a diabolical instigation after their deaths. And I myself should be cursed unless I correct their errors and hand down the truth in this science, just as this true art <note>original: "ars uera"</note> best requires. For this mastery...

It does not require a hidden language, nor one that is entirely plain. Returning therefore to our purpose, we say that those who place the art in the "spirits" <note>In alchemy, "spirits" refers to volatile substances that vaporize when heated, such as mercury, sulfur, and arsenic.</note> are divided in many ways. Some assert that the Stone of the Philosophers must be sought from Quicksilver <note>original: "Argento uiuo"</note>, others from Sulfur, and its relative Arsenic. And some others seek it from Marcasite <note>A common iron sulfide mineral often mistaken for gold or silver ore.</note>, some from Tutty <note>Zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces.</note> and Magnesia, and some from Sal Ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride, used as a flux and for cleaning metals.</note>. Those, however, who place it in the "bodies" <note>The "bodies" refer to the solid, non-volatile metals.</note>, some say it is in Lead, others in any of the other bodies; others indeed in Glass, and some in Gemstones, and others in various kinds of salts and alums, and nitres and boraxes; and others in every kind of vegetable matter. And to every one of these proponents, there is an adversary according to his own supposition. And he who opposes these believes himself to be simply opposing the Art itself. And for the most part, we find the sects of both sides to be void of reason.

### Reasons of those denying the art is placed in sulfur. Chapter XIII.

Certain people, therefore, supposing the art to be found in sulfur, spent their labor on sulfur, and being ignorant of the perfection of its preparation, they left that preparation incomplete. For they believed that cleansing and purification alone would be the perfection of the preparation; this, however, is done through sublimation <note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify substances.</note>. Therefore, it was brought to their intention to think that sublimation alone in sulfur constitutes the perfection of its preparation, and they introduced the same thinking regarding its companion, namely arsenic. Coming therefore to the "projection" <note>The final stage of the alchemical process where the "Stone" is cast upon a base metal to transmute it into gold or silver.</note>, which is

### Refutation of the preceding arguments. Chapter 14.

We respond to them briefly, and we say that in this matter they understand little and have very little wisdom, because they suppose that sulfur alone is our material. Even if this supposition were true, they are nonetheless deceived in the method of preparation, because they believe that sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again, used for purification</note> alone is sufficient. They are like a child who, from the beginning of his birth until old age, is shut up in a house, not thinking the width of the world extends beyond the width of his own house, or beyond what he can see with his eye inside that house. For these men have not applied their labor to many different stones; therefore, they could not perceive from what our medicine <note>The Elixir or Philosopher's Stone</note> may be drawn out and from what it may not, especially since they have excused their hands from an abundance of labors. It is only right, then, that they should be ignorant of what completes the work and what does not. But as for why their work was diminished, we say it is because they left the "burning quality" and the "flight" <note>Volatility; the tendency of a substance to evaporate when heated</note> within the sulfur, which not only fail to perfect the work, but actually scatter and destroy it.

### Arguments of those denying the art based on the spirits, together with the fixing of bodies, and their refutation. Chapter XVII.

There are also others striving to "fix" <note>to make a volatile substance stable under heat</note> the spirits within the bodies of metals with no other preparation preceding this; but a similar distressing delusion has brought them sorrow and despair. They are compelled by this to believe that this science does not exist and to argue against it. Indeed, the cause of their confusion and disbelief is this: that during the melting of the bodies, those spirits leave them and do not adhere to them; rather, they flee the harshness of the fire, while only the bodies remain in it. This happens because the spirits cannot endure the pressure of the fire's cruelty due to their "flight," which has not been removed from them. 

Similarly, delusion sometimes occurs because the bodies themselves flee the fire along with the spirits. This happens when the spirits, not being fixed, have not adhered inseparably to the depths of the bodies, since the high quantity of the volatile overcomes the quantity of the fixed. Hence, they argue just as the first group did, and we respond to them in the same way. It is certainly necessary for these spirits <note>In alchemy, "spirits" usually refers to volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic that can evaporate or "flee" when heated.</note> to be created; however, it is not possible for them to adhere usefully to bodies if they are not fixed. On the contrary, they flee and leave those bodies impure. Furthermore, it is not possible for them to enter the bodies once they have been fixed, since they have then become like earth, which does not melt. Even when they appear fixed while enclosed within bodies, they are not truly so; either they depart while the bodies remain, or both flee together. Therefore, since it is impossible to find this art by any means in a more closely related matter, it will certainly not be found in a more remote one—thus, it is found nowhere. Our response to this is that they do not know everything that can be known about this subject, and therefore they do not find the complete result of their work; thus, they mistakenly blame the art for their own lack of strength and insufficient knowledge.

->*The arguments of those who deny the art based on the nature of the bodies, and*<-

However, some have placed the art within the bodies themselves. Yet when they came to the actual work, they were deceived. They thought that both types of lead—namely, the livid <note>original: "liuidum," referring to common lead (Saturn).</note> and the white <note>original: "album," referring to tin (Jupiter).</note>—though not of a pure whiteness, closely resembled and approached the nature of the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note>. They believed the livid lead was very close to the Sun and slightly to the Moon, while the white lead was very close to the Moon and slightly to the Sun. For this reason, some of them, thinking that tin (or Jupiter) was very similar to the Moon—differing only in its "creaking" sound <note>The "cry of tin," a distinctive crackling sound made when bending a bar of tin.</note>, its softness, and the speed at which it melts—believed it was easy to melt due to an excess of its humidity. They similarly thought its softness and the creaking of its parts were caused by the fugitive substance of quicksilver <note>Mercury</note> trapped within it. They exposed it to fire, and by calcining it <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</note>, they kept it in as much heat as it could tolerate until it turned white in its powdered form. Afterward, when they wished to reduce it back to metal, they were unable to do so, and thus they judged the task to be impossible.

And some of these practitioners reduced a portion of that substance, and they found in it a screeching sound <note>original: "stridorem"; likely referring to the "tin-cry," a characteristic sound made when bending tin</note> as before, as well as softness and a tendency to melt quickly. And so, others among them, wishing to provide it with hardness and a delay in melting by adding hard bodies <note>Refers to adding harder metals like iron or copper to the alloy</note>, fell into a delusion; for whatever hard bodies were mixed with it were shattered by it, and no preparation helped them in this. Therefore, since they could not prepare it with hard bodies or with fire, they excused themselves for the long delay in discovering the art, because they believed it impossible. By arguing persistently against the art because of this, they asserted that it did not exist. Furthermore, certain others, adding many medicines <note>original: "medicamina"; in alchemy, these are chemical reagents or elixirs intended to transform the metal</note>, saw that these caused no change and were not suitable for it, but rather corrupted it and acted against their purpose. For this reason, they threw away their books, turned their heads away, and said that the true and divine art was frivolous. Meeting these people, we respond with our first answer.

### The arguments of those who deny the art based on the mixing of hard bodies with hard, and soft with soft. Chapter 20.

Others, however, mixing hard bodies with hard and soft with soft, wished for the bodies to be mutually transmuted and to transmute one another because of their similarity. Indeed, some of them last longer in the mixture, while others last less, as has been sufficiently determined by us. Therefore, these delusions arising from ignorance cause such people to distrust this art and to argue that it does not exist.

### *The arguments of those who deny that the art is based on the mixing of hard substances with soft, and perfect substances with imperfect. Chapter XXI.*

Others, however, inquiring more intimately and deeply into this matter, have pondered and exerted their ingenuity, wishing to find a way so that hard things, when united with soft, might permanently harden them; and that perfect things, when joined with imperfect, might lead them back to perfection; and generally, that they might be transformed by one another and transform each other through a stable transmutation. And for this reason, they wished to find a similarity and affinity between them, sometimes indeed through medicines <note>In alchemy, a "medicine" or "elixir" refers to a substance capable of curing the "sickness" of base metals to turn them into gold.</note>, and at other times through the administration of fire—by thinning those things that are coarse, such as Venus <note>Copper</note> and Mars <note>Iron</note>, and by thickening those that are subtle, such as Jupiter <note>Tin</note> and those similar to it. And some of them, believing they could complete this administration, were deceived in the mixing of these hard bodies, either because they made the result entirely brittle, or entirely too soft (not being altered by the hard), or too hard (not being altered by the soft). And thus they did not find a suitable agreement, and for that reason, they denied that the Art exists.

### *The arguments of those who deny that the art is based on the extraction of the soul, or the governance of fire. Chapter XXII.*

Others indeed, looking even more intimately and deeply, wished to alter bodies by the extraction of their souls <note>The "soul" (anima) was considered the volatile essence or "tincture" of a metal that gave it its specific properties.</note>, and with the soul extracted, to treat all other things similarly. And their experience was not able to reach this goal, but they were deceived in their intention, judging by this that the Art could not be found. Others truly, attempting to perfect these things by fire alone, were deceived in their opinion because they did not know how to arrive at that result. And these men, for this reason, thought the Art did not exist. To all of whom we object, just as we did to the first group.

## The arguments of those who deny the art is based in glass and gems, and their refutation. Chapter XXIII.

Those who have placed the art in Glass and Gems have found by experience that alterations cannot be made in [metallic] bodies through Glass and Gems. This is because nothing alters what it does not penetrate; yet neither Glass nor Gems penetrate, and therefore they do not alter. Even if they have attempted to unite Glass with those bodies—though this can scarcely be done—they still do not achieve their purpose. Because they make Glass out of the bodies, they estimate that this error applies to the entire art, and thus they argue that the art does not exist. To these we respond: they are working with improper material, and therefore, reaching an improper conclusion, they cannot destroy this art based on their own errors.

## The arguments of those who deny the art is based in middle minerals, or vegetables, or the mixture of any other things. Chapter XXIIII.

There are also others who suppose this art is to be found in Salts and Alums, Nitres and Boraxes <note>These "middle minerals" were often used as fluxes or cleaning agents, but Geber argues they are not the primary material for transmutation.</note>. It is possible, nevertheless, for some alteration to be found in all these things, but it is very remote and extremely laborious. Furthermore, for those who suppose it is in all other growing things <note>Referring to organic or "vegetable" alchemy using plants.</note>, it is proven to be even more laborious. Therefore, those who place the art in all vegetables propose something that is indeed possible, but not for them, because...

They would sooner fail in their labor than it would be possible for the work to be completed. However, all those previously mentioned, who are in error, posited only one single material of their own and assumed no other besides it. All of these men have indeed now been refuted. Yet many others—an almost infinite number—who create compositions of all these things, or of certain things in varying proportions, proceed in ignorance and lack of knowledge. Their error extends into infinity, because the diversity of proportions in mixable things is infinite, and the diversity of the mixable materials themselves is infinite. In both of these infinities, it is possible to err infinitely—sometimes by excess, sometimes by deficiency—and in these cases, correction is possible. But we, sparing ourselves the length and tediousness of long speeches, do not wish to dwell upon infinite details, since we shall hand down a universal science in brief statements. By these, they will be able to clearly amend the infinity of their errors and correct them. which we also allow to be called "dry water." However, we have divided the stinking spirit <note>original: "spiritum foetentem"; likely referring to sulfur due to its odor</note>, for it is white in its hidden state, and both red and black in the mastery of this work. ### *On the natural principles of metals, according to the opinion*
### *of the moderns and the author. Chapter XXVI.*

Others, however, have said otherwise: that the principle was not quicksilver <term>Quicksilver: Mercury</term> in its own nature, but altered and converted into its own earth, and sulfur likewise altered and changed into earth. Whence they said that the principle was something other than the "stinking spirit" and the "fugitive spirit" <note>original: "spiritus fugitiuus"; a term for volatile substances like mercury that evaporate or "flee" when heated</note> in the intention of nature. And the reason they were moved to this was because they do not find in the mines of silver or other metals anything that is quicksilver in its own nature, nor anything that is likewise sulfur; rather, they find each of those separated by themselves in their own...
