<note>page 48</note>

in its own mine within its own nature. And similarly, they affirm this also through another line of reasoning. They say there is no passage from one contrary to another contrary except through a middle disposition <note>a transitional state or "mean" between two extremes</note>. Therefore, since this is the case, they are forced to admit and believe that there is no passage from the softness of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti viui"; mercury</note> to the hardness of any of the metals, except through a disposition that lies between their hardness and softness. 

But in the mines, they do not find anything in which this middle disposition is preserved; therefore, by this reasoning, they are compelled to believe that quicksilver and sulfur in their own nature are not the primary principle intended by nature. Rather, it is something else that follows from the alteration of their essences at the root of nature into an earthy substance. 

And the method is this: first, each of them is converted to an earthy nature, and from both of these earthy natures, a very thin smoke <note>original: "fumus"; often used interchangeably with "vapor" or "exhalation" in alchemy</note> is released by the multiplied heat in the bowels of the earth. This dual smoke is the immediate matter of metals. When this smoke has been "cooked" <term>decocted: the process of refining or ripening a substance through steady heat</term> by the temperate heat of the mine, it is converted into the nature of a certain earth. For that reason, it undergoes a certain fixation. Then, water flowing through the bowels of the mine and the sponginess of the earth dissolves it, and is uniformly united to it in a natural and firm union. 

Therefore, those who hold this opinion have said that the water flowing through the passages of the earth finds a dissolvable substance from the substance of the earth in its bowels; it dissolves that substance and unites uniformly with it, until both the substance of the earth dissolved in the bowels and the flowing water that dissolves it become one through a natural union. To such a mixture, all the elements come according to their due natural proportion, and they are mixed "through the smallest parts" <note>original: "per minima"; a physical theory suggesting substances mix at the most microscopic level</note> until they create a uniform mixture. And this mixture, through successive decoction in the mine, is thickened and hardened, and becomes a metal. And these people, although they are close to the truth, do not yet grasp the pure truth.

# THE SUM OF PERFECTION BY GEBER

### Division of the discussion concerning the three principles, namely Sulphur, Arsenic, and Quicksilver. Chapter XXVII.

We have already determined in a universal discourse the natural principles of metals. It remains, therefore, that we now set down a chapter for each individual principle. Since there are three—Sulphur, Arsenic, and Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum uiuum," literally "living silver"</note>—we shall first assign a chapter to Sulphur. Second, to Arsenic. Third, to Quicksilver. Then, we shall set down a specific chapter for each of the metals which are the effects of these principles, according to how they are produced by the work of nature. From there, passing on to those things which are the foundations of this mastery <note>The "mastery" or "magistery" refers to the professional skill and secret knowledge of the alchemist</note> and their operations, we shall assign the causes of all these things.

---

### Concerning Sulphur. Chapter XXVIII.

We say, therefore, that Sulphur is the fatness of the earth, thickened in the mine of the earth by a temperate decoction <note>A process of heating or "cooking" within the earth's crust over long periods</note> until it becomes hardened and dry; and when it has been hardened, it is called Sulphur. Indeed, sulphur has a homogeneous and very strong composition, and is of a uniform substance in its parts, being "homeomerous" <term>homeomerous: a philosophical term meaning that every part of a substance has the same nature as the whole</term>, because it is homogeneous. Therefore, its oil is not taken away from it by distillation, as it is from other things that possess oil. Those, therefore, who seek to calcine <term>calcine: to reduce a mineral to powder by heat, usually to remove volatile components</term> it without losing any of its substance worth caring about, labor in vain; for it is not calcined except by great industry, and by wasting much of its substance. For out of a hundred parts, you will scarcely reserve three for yourself sufficiently after calcination. Similarly, it cannot be fixed <note>To "fix" a substance in alchemy is to make a volatile or liquid material solid and resistant to fire</note> unless it is first calcined; it can, however, be mixed, and a little...

### On Arsenic. Chapter XXIX.

It remains for us to determine the nature of Arsenic <note>original: "Arsenico"</note> at present. We say, therefore, that it is of a subtle matter, and similar to sulfur; for that reason, it need not be defined differently than sulfur. However, it differs from sulfur in this: that it is easily a tincture <note>A substance used to change the color or quality of a metal.</note> of whiteness, but only with great difficulty a tincture of redness; whereas sulfur is easily a tincture of redness, but only with great difficulty of whiteness. Furthermore, there are two kinds of sulfur and Arsenic: namely, the yellow <note>original: "citrinum"</note> and the red, which are useful to this art, while many other kinds are not. Arsenic is fixed <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note> just like sulfur. Indeed, the sublimation <note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification.</note> of both is better when performed from the calxes <note>original: "calcibus"; the powdery metallic oxide remaining after a metal has been burned or roasted.</note> of metals. However, sulfur and Arsenic are not the perfect matter of this work. For they are not complete unto perfection, though they may provide an aid to perfection in certain cases. One should choose that which is bright, scaly, and easily split.

->On the Sun, or Gold. Chapter XXXII.<-

We have provided you, in the general chapter, with a summary of the intentions regarding metals; however, we shall now provide you with a specific discourse on each one. And first, concerning Gold. We say, therefore, that Gold is a metallic body, lemon-yellow <note>original: "citrinum"</note>, heavy, mute <note>meaning it does not ring loudly when struck, unlike copper</note>, shining, equally digested in the belly of the earth, washed for a very long time by mineral water, extensible under the hammer, fusible, and able to withstand the trial of the ash-cup <note>the "cineritium" or cupellation process used to refine precious metals</note> and the cement <note>a dry refining process using corrosive salts</note>. From this definition, therefore, you may conclude that a thing is not gold unless it possesses all the causes and differences of the definition of gold. Nevertheless, whatever metal it thoroughly colors yellow, brings to equality, and cleanses, it makes gold out of every kind of metal. And therefore, through the work of nature, we weigh and consider that copper <note>original: "æs"</note> can be changed into gold by art. For we have seen in copper mines, from which water flowed, that the water carried with it very thin scales of copper. And by its long and continuous flow, it washed and cleansed them. Then, when the water ceased to flow, we saw these scales cooked out by the heat of the sun in dry sand for a period of three years, among which most true gold was found. We estimated, therefore, that they had been cleansed by the benefit of the water, and by the heat of the Sun in the dryness of the sand, they were equally digested and reached a state of equality. Thus, imitating nature as far as we are able, we likewise alter [metals], yet we are not able to follow nature in every respect. Gold is also the most precious of metals, and it is a tincture of redness, because it colors and transforms every body. It is calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> and dissolved without utility <note>Geber likely suggests that for the alchemist, gold is already perfect and does not need these processes to improve itself, though they are used in other operations</note>, and it is a medicine that gladdens and preserves the body in youth. ->On the Moon, or Silver. Chapter XXXIII.<-

The chapter on the Sun <note>Gold</note> having been set forth, let us direct our discourse to the Moon, known by the common name of silver. It is, therefore, a tincture of whiteness; it hardens Jupiter <note>Tin</note> through the art, converts it to itself, and mixes with the Sun <note>Gold</note> without breaking it, though in a trial without the art, it does not remain with it. When placed over the fumes of sharp substances, such as vinegar, sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note>, and verjuice <note>the juice of unripened grapes</note>, a marvelous celestial blue color is produced. It is a noble body, but diminished from the nobility of gold. Its ore is found in specific veins, and sometimes it has an ore confused with other bodies, and that is not as noble. It is likewise calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> and dissolved with great labor but with no utility.

However, it has a flaw: it breaks every body <note>referring to the brittleness or "cry" of tin when alloyed</note> except for Saturn <note>Lead</note> and the purest Sun <note>Gold</note>. And Jupiter adheres closely to the Sun and the Moon <note>Silver</note>, and for that reason, it does not easily depart from them through the trials <note>original: "per examina," referring to cupellation or refining tests</note>. It receives the tincture of redness, shines within it with an inestimable brightness, and acquires weight in the mastery of this art. It is hardened and cleansed more easily than Saturn. And whoever knows how to remove its flaw of brittleness will rejoice to suddenly enjoy its profit. For it is compatible with the Sun and the Moon, and shall never be separated from them.

### Concerning Venus, or Copper. Chapter XXXVI.

Let our discourse at present be concerning Venus <note>The alchemical name for Copper</note>. It is a metallic body, livid, participating in a dark redness, ignitable <note>capable of being heated to a glow</note>, fusible, extensible under the hammer, yet fleeing from the ash-cupel <note>original: "cineritium," a refining furnace</note> and cementation <note>a process for purifying gold</note>. Venus, therefore (as has been told), in the depths of its substance, claims the color and essence of gold, yet it is hammered and heated like silver and gold. Therefore, you should take the secret from it, because it is a medium between the Sun and the Moon, and it happens that its nature is easily converted to either one; it is of good conversion and requires little labor. It agrees vehemently with tutia <note>term: tutia; a crude zinc oxide found on the walls of smelting furnaces</note>, which colors it yellow with a good yellowness <note>original: "citrinat," referring to the creation of brass</note>, and from this you may draw profit. We are thus excused by it from the labors of hardening and igniting it. Therefore, you should choose it above the other imperfect metals in the minor and middle work, but in the "Great Work" <note>original: "in maiori," the final stage of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> not at all. However, it has this flaw compared to Jupiter: it tarnishes <note>literally "turns blue-black"</note> easily and receives infection from sharp and acrid substances <note>referring to the formation of verdigris</note>, and to eradicate that is no easy craft, but rather a profound one.

### Concerning Mars, or Iron. Chapter XXXVII.

The description of Mars <note>The alchemical name for Iron</note>, and its entire secret, is derived from the work of nature; for it is a metallic body of a dull, leaden color, with a very slight hint of red, sharing in a non-pure whiteness. It is hard, combustible <note>original: "ignibile," referring here to its tendency to spark or oxidize</note>, and fusible, though not with a smooth or easy flow. It is extensible under the hammer and highly resonant. Mars is, however, difficult to work with because of the weakness of its fusion. If it is melted by a medicine <note>An alchemical elixir or reagent</note> that changes its nature, it may be joined to the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note>, and cannot be separated by the trial <note>The cupellation or assaying process</note> without great industry. But if it is prepared and joined without its fixed nature being changed—only its impurity being removed—it cannot be separated by any artifice. Therefore, the tincture of redness <note>Gold-making</note> is easily achieved from it, but whiteness <note>Silver-making</note> is achieved with difficulty. When it is joined without being altered, it does not change the color of the mixture but increases it in quantity.

Among all bodies, therefore, Jupiter <note>Tin</note> is transformed into the solar and lunar body most splendidly, clearly, brightly, and perfectly. But in it, the work is of easy handling but long labor. After that, Venus <note>Copper</note> is chosen, though of less perfect transformation; it is of more difficult handling, but of shorter labor than Jupiter. Saturn <note>Lead</note>, after Venus, has a perfection in transmutation diminished from hers; it is of easy handling, but of the longest labor. Mars, however, stands among the others as having the least perfection in transmutation, being of the most difficult handling and the longest labor. 

Therefore, whichever bodies are further removed from speed of liquefaction <note>i.e., those with higher melting points</note> are found to be of more difficult handling in the work of transmutation. Such are Venus and Mars. Those that melt more easily are easier to work; those that melt most easily are the easiest. Furthermore, whichever metals participate more in "lividness" <note>leaden or dull coloring</note> and infection from the earth are found to require greater labor and yield less perfection. These various degrees of perfection, which we determined a little earlier, are found in the works of the minor and middle operations.

Geber explains that a metal's melting point and purity determine the ease and success of the alchemical process.</summary>

Perfection, truly, consists of the consideration of those things by which one arrives at it, and from the consideration of the things that assist it, and from the consideration of the thing itself which ultimately perfects the work, and by which it is known whether the mastery <note>Latin: *magisterium*, referring to the completed alchemical process or the "Philosopher's Stone" itself</note> was in a state of perfection or not.

The consideration of those things by which the completion of the work is reached is the consideration of the manifest substance, and of the manifest colors, and of the weight in each of the bodies to be transformed, and of those bodies which are not to be changed from the root of their nature without that artifice, and likewise the consideration of those in their root with the artifice. ### On Sublimation, and why it was invented. Chapter 39.

Following our purpose, therefore, we speak of sublimation <note>Latin: sublimatio; the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</note>. And the reason for its invention was because our ancestors did not find, nor have we, nor will those who come after us find anything that could be united with the bodies <note>metals</note> except for spirits alone, or something that contained the nature of both body and spirit within itself. And they saw that when these were cast upon the bodies without their being cleansed, they either gave imperfect colors or entirely corrupted, burned, blackened, and defiled them. And this occurred according to the diversity of the spirits themselves. For some are "burning," such as sulfur, arsenic, and marcasite <note>Latin: marchesita; likely iron pyrites or similar metallic ores</note>, and these indeed corrupt entirely. Others, however, do not burn, such as every kind of tutty <note>Latin: tutiae; zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</note>, and these indeed give imperfect colors. This is because those things which burn, blacken, and defile do so for two reasons. One is because the "burning oiliness" of sulfur—whose property is to be easily inflamed, and through inflammation to be blackened, and consequently to blacken other things—has not been removed from them. The other reason is the "earthiness," which likewise was not removed from them. In those things in which a perfect color is not given, the cause is the earthiness, which makes the color leaden or dull. Burning can also create a leaden color. And therefore, we have applied our ingenuity

For when fire elevates a substance, it always raises the finer parts and leaves behind the coarser ones. From this it is clear that through sublimation, the <term>spirit</term><note>In alchemy, "spirits" refer to volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, and arsenic that can be vaporized.</note> is cleansed of the earthiness which both hindered its ability to enter other materials and gave it a foul color. You will find this same thing in sulfur if you experiment with it. Because we have seen an adherence to bodies with alteration in no other things than in these spirits, we were excused by no other cause from the necessity of preparing them by cleansing them through sublimation; therefore, this was the necessary cause for its invention. Let us therefore describe the entire order of sublimation without omission, and the reason for it.

### FOURTH PART OF THE FIRST BOOK

If arsenic or sulfur is to be sublimated <note>Sublimation is the alchemical process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then collecting the purified solid as it cools at the top of the vessel.</note>, it is necessary that they be sublimated by a mild fire. Because these substances have very subtle parts joined uniformly with coarse parts, their entire substance would otherwise rise without any purification—indeed, it would be blackened and scorched. Therefore, so that one may separate the unclean, earthy substance, it is necessary to discover two types of ingenuity: namely, the correct proportion of the fire, and the method of cleansing through mixing with dregs <note>original: "fecibus"; refers to the solid residue or "lees" used to anchor the substance during heating.</note>. This is because mixing with the dregs catches the coarse parts and keeps them pressed down at the bottom of the aludels <note>term: aludel (a pear-shaped earthenware bottle used as a condenser in the sublimation process)</note>, not permitting them to climb upward.

For this reason, it is necessary for the craftsman to apply a triple degree of fire to the sublimation. 

The first degree is proportioned in such a way that only the altered, cleaner, and brighter parts rise through it, until the craftsman clearly sees them being cleansed of their earthy foulness. 

The second degree is such that whatever remains of their pure essence within the dregs may be sublimated with a greater expression of fire—namely, with the ignition of the aludel and the dregs themselves, which he will be able to see with his own eyes. 

The third degree is that a very weak fire should be administered, without dregs, to that which has already been sublimated from the dregs and purified. This is done so that hardly any of it rises; that which does rise from it is a most subtle thing which is worthless in this work, because that is the substance through which scorching <note>original: "adustio"; the unwanted burning or oxidation of the material.</note> occurs in sulfurs. 

Therefore, the entire intention of sublimation is this: that once its earthiness is removed through the proper administration of fire, and once that most subtle and smoky part (which brings about scorching and corruption) is likewise cast away from it, there remains for us that part which consists in balance. This part performs a simple fusion over the fire without any scorching, and without fleeing from the fire or bursting into flame. 

That the most subtle part is indeed the cause of scorching is proven by the most manifest arguments. For fire converts into its own nature each of those things which is most closely related to it, because...

By these points, therefore, it is clear that our discourse is truthful.

### *On the dross of metallic bodies, the spirits to be added in sublimation, and their quantity and quality. Chapter 41.*

The proof of the management of dross <note>original: "fecum"; refers to the solid residue or impurities left after a process</note> with its proper proportion is this: that a material should be chosen with which the spirits to be sublimated are most compatible, and with which they may be most deeply intermingled. This is because the material to which they are more closely united is more powerful in retaining the dross of the substances being sublimated than one to which they are not. The proof of this is sufficiently rational and manifest. 

The proof that the management of dross is necessary is this: if the sulfur or arsenic to be sublimated were not joined with the dross of some fixed thing, then it would be necessary for them to ascend with their entire substance, unpurified. Those who are practiced in sublimations know by experience that we speak the truth. 

The proof that the management of such dross is necessary—specifically those with which the substances to be sublimated are compatible and united in their depths—is because if the dross were not mixed down to the smallest parts <note>original: "per minima"; a natural philosophy term referring to the smallest possible particles of a substance</note>, then the same thing would happen as if they had no dross at all. That is to say, their entire essence would ascend without any purification, just as they ascend with their whole substance when without dross; therefore, it must necessarily happen similarly to substances sublimated from dross to which they are not united. Experience knows this to be true for anyone who has seen and known this, because when he sublimated from a thing foreign to the nature of bodies, he sublimated

For in a small quantity, a small fire is drawn out for perfection; in a large quantity, a large fire; in a greater, a greater.

# THE SUM OF PERFECTION BY GEBER. 63

### On moderating the fire in Sublimation.
### Chapter XLII.

But since fire is not a thing that can be measured <note>The author refers to the lack of thermometers or precise heat gauges in the medieval period; heat was judged by sight and touch.</note>, it often happens that errors occur in its use when a person is not experienced, arising as much from the variety of furnaces and the wood to be burned as from the vessels and their fitting together. Concerning all these matters, it is necessary for the attentive craftsman to be diligent. 

However, we provide a general rule: first, it is useful to express only the "wateriness" <note>original: "aqueitatem"; referring to the initial moisture or volatile impurities</note> from the substances to be sublimated <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again in a purer form</term> using a small fire. Once this is removed, if anything rises because of that heat, the fire should not be increased at the start, so that the most subtle part may be carried off by the weakest fire and set aside, as this part is the cause of scorching <note>original: "adustionis"</note>. 

But when little or nothing more rises (which you can test by inserting a cotton wick into the upper hole of the aludel <term>Aludel: a pear-shaped chemical vessel used as a condenser in the sublimation process</term>), the fire beneath it should be strengthened. The experience with the wick will show you how strong the fire ought to be. For if only a little of the substance comes out, or if it is clean, the fire is still too low; therefore, let it be increased. If, however, much comes out and it is impure, then the fire is excessive; therefore, let it be reduced. But if it is clean and plentiful, the correct proportion has been found. 

Whether it is clean or impure will be known by pulling out the wick that was placed in the hole of the aludel. According to the quantity, cleanliness, or impurity of the sublimated material the craftsman sees adhering to the wick, he will be able to reason out and find the necessary proportional fire throughout the entire sublimation, and from this, he will find the correct adjustment of the fire without error. 

A better method for this is to use scales of iron or burnt copper. These, because they lack harmful moisture, easily absorb and unite with sulfur or arsenic. However, only the experienced practitioner knows the way of this method.

# FOURTH PART OF THE FIRST BOOK

### On avoiding errors regarding the quantity of dregs and the arrangement of the furnace in the sublimation of sulfur and arsenic. Also on constructing the furnace and choosing the wood. Chapter XLIII.

It is therefore necessary for us to guide the craftsman in all matters where one might err through ignorance during the sublimation <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a solid substance until it turns into vapor and then collects again as a solid in a cooler part of the apparatus, used here to purify chemicals.</note> of these two spirits <note>original: "spirituum"; in alchemy, "spirits" refers to volatile substances like sulfur and arsenic that vaporize easily.</note>. Let us first state that if he uses too many dregs <note>original: "feces"; the solid remains or impure matter mixed with the chemical.</note>, then unless he increases the fire proportionally, nothing of the substance to be sublimated will rise. How he may find that proportion has already been sufficiently explained to him. 

And if he uses a small quantity of dregs, or does not use dregs made from the calx <note>original: "calce"; a powder produced by heating a metal or mineral to high temperatures.</note> of bodies, then if he does not find the correct proportion, the substance to be sublimated will rise along with its entire crude mass. I have likewise provided sufficient instruction for finding this. 

Regarding the furnace, it is similarly possible to err. For a large furnace gives a large fire, while a small one gives a small fire, provided that the wood and the openings of its vents <note>original: "auricularum"; literally "little ears," referring to the air holes or intake vents of the furnace.</note> are proportional. If, therefore, he places a large quantity of the substance to be sublimated into a small furnace, he will not be able to produce a fire sufficient for its elevation. If, however, he puts a small quantity into a large furnace, he will ruin the sublimation because of the excess of heat. 

Similarly, a thick-walled furnace gives a concentrated and strong fire, while a thin-walled one gives a thin and weak fire, in which matters it is likewise possible to err. Furthermore, a furnace with spacious vents gives a clear and large fire, while one with narrow vents gives a weak one. Also, if the distance of the vessel <note>The vessel here refers to the aludel, a pear-shaped pot used in sublimation.</note> from the ledges <note>original: "spondilibus"; the internal supports or rims within the furnace that hold the vessel.</note> of the furnace is greater when it is fitted, it will give a large fire; if it is smaller, it will give a smaller fire. In all these things, it is very easy to err. 

The correction for these things, therefore, is that the furnace should be constructed according to the intensity of the fire required: namely, thick-walled with free-flowing vents and with a large distance between the aludel <term>Aludel: a series of earthenware pots used as receivers in the sublimation process</term> vessel and the ledges of the furnace, if a large fire is required. If, however, a moderate fire is needed, let him find a moderate proportion in all these things; but if

### *From what material and in what form the Aludel vessel should be made. Chapter 44.*

The intention for the Aludel <term>Aludel: a pear-shaped subliming pot used in alchemy to collect vapors</term> vessel is that it should be fashioned as a thick glass vessel. For it is not effective if made of another material, unless perhaps it were of a substance similar to thick glass. For only glass and its like, since they lack pores, are able to hold the spirits <note>original: "spiritus" — volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or arsenic</note> so that they do not flee and be destroyed by the fire. There is no other material, because through their pores the spirits are successively diminished and vanish. Nor are metals effective in this, because the spirits, on account of their friendship and affinity with them, penetrate the metals and unite with them; wherefore, passing through them, they vanish, which is clearly proven by those things determined by us. By necessity and experience it has been found that we have spoken the truth; therefore, we are not excused by anything from the adoption of glass in the composition of the Aludel. Therefore, let a round glass shell be fashioned, the bottom of which should be of small curvature, and in the middle of its joints let a glass belt be formed surrounding it, and upon that belt let a wall be founded...

# FOURTH PART OF THE FIRST BOOK

### On the sublimation of Mercury, or Quicksilver.
#### Chapter 45.

Now, indeed, let us define the entire purpose of the sublimation <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify it.</note> of quicksilver. Its completion is the highest purification of its earthiness and the removal of its wateriness. We are, however, excused from the labor of removing its combustibility <note>original: "adustionis"</note>, because it does not possess any. We say, therefore, that the ingenious method for separating its superfluous earth is to mix it with things for which it has no affinity, and to repeat its sublimation from them many times. Among this class of things are talc, and the lime <note>calx: a powder produced by heating a substance to high temperatures</note> of eggshells, and of white marble. Likewise, very finely ground glass and every kind of prepared salt may be used. For by these it is cleansed. But by other things having an affinity with it—unless they are the "bodies of perfection" <note>A reference to gold or silver, which alchemists believed were the only metals free of corrupting sulfur</note>—it is instead corrupted, because all such things possess a sulfurous quality <note>original: "sulphureitatem"</note> which, ascending with the mercury during sublimation, corrupts it. You can see the proof of this in experience: if you sublime it from tin or from lead, you will see it infected with blackness after the sublimation. Therefore, its sublimation is better achieved through those things with which it does not harmonize. It would be better with those it does harmonize with, if only they did not have that sulfurous quality. For this reason, sublimation from lime is better than from all other things, since it harmonizes little with the mercury and has no sulfurous quality.

The method for removing its superfluous wateriness is this: when it is mixed with the limes from which it is to be sublimed, it should be ground and mixed with them by "imbibition" <note>The process of soaking a dry substance with liquid until it is saturated</note> until nothing of the mercury appears. Afterward, the wateriness of the imbibition should be removed over a very slow fire. As that moisture recedes, the wateriness of the quicksilver recedes along with it. However, let the fire be so gentle that the entire substance of the quicksilver does not ascend because of it. Therefore, through the manifold repetition of imbibition with grinding, and

By gentle roasting <note>original: "assatione," a slow heating process used to remove moisture</note>, its greater wateriness is destroyed, the remainder of which is removed through the repetition of sublimation. For a fixed part of it adheres to the dregs, and it could never be separated from them by any kind of ingenuity. Or, after that, you may fix a part of it, and we will expressly deliver the method of its fixation to you in the following sections. 

And when you have fixed it, then repeat the sublimation of the remaining part over it, so that it may likewise be fixed; and keep what you will test over the fire. If it yields a good fusion <note>meaning it melts properly</note>, then you have administered sufficient sublimation to it. But if not, add to it some portion of sublimated quicksilver <note>term: quicksilver (mercury)</note>, and repeat the sublimation until it is finished. If it possesses a clear and most white color, and is transparent, then you have cleansed it well; if not, you have not. Therefore, do not be negligent in its preparation which is done through sublimation, because as the cleansing is, so follows the perfection through it, in its projection <note>term: projection (the act of casting the alchemical catalyst onto a base metal to transform it)</note> upon each of the imperfect bodies, and upon the unprepared quicksilver itself. 

Whence it happens that some form iron, some indeed lead, some through it form Venus <note>note: "Venus" is the alchemical name for copper</note>, and some form tin. This happens because of negligence in purification, sometimes of that substance alone, sometimes in the sulfur mixed with it, or its companion. If, therefore, you have cleansed it by direct sublimation and perfected it, it will be a firm and perfect tincture of whiteness, to which there is no equal.

### On the Sublimation of Marcasite. Chapter XLVI.

The highest intention of the sublimation of quicksilver having been sufficiently delivered, let us now approach the sublimation of Marcasite <note>term: Marcasite (in medieval alchemy, this often referred to various metallic sulfides, particularly iron pyrites or bismuth)</note> itself. There are, however, two methods for its sublimation.

# FOURTH PART OF THE FIRST BOOK

The first process is indeed completed without ignition <note>The application of high heat or "firing" the vessel until it glows</note>, while the other is done with ignition. This is because the substance has a dual nature. One part is pure sulfur in its natural state, and the other is "mortified" mercury <note>original: "argentum vivum mortificatum"; mercury that has been chemically altered or "killed" to lose its fluid, metallic form</note>. The first part is useful in the same way sulfur is. The second is useful as mercury that has been mortified and moderately prepared. Let us therefore take up this latter part, because through it we are spared from needing the superior mercury and the labor of its mortification. Therefore, the entire method of its sublimation <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again in a cooler part of the apparatus</term> is as follows: it should be ground, placed in an aludel <note>original: "aludele"; a pear-shaped laboratory vessel used in sublimation</note>, and its sulfur should be sublimated without ignition, always removing what rises from it very frequently for the reason stated, and increasing the strength of the fire until the ignition of the aludel.

The first sublimation of marcasite <note>original: "marchesitæ"; a term used historically for various sulfide minerals, often iron pyrites</note> ought to take place in the sublimation vessel until the sulfur has departed, and afterwards proceed in that vessel successively and in an orderly fashion until everything consisting of sulfur within it has exited. You will be able to prove this by these manifest experiments: for when all of its sulfur has been raised, you will see the color of what is sublimated after it change into a very pure white, mixed with a most clear and pleasant celestial blue color. There is also another way: because that which is of the nature of sulfur will be consumed by fire and give off a flame like sulfur. However, that which is sublimated second after it will neither be set on fire nor show any properties of sulfur, but rather those of mortified mercury in the repetition of the sublimation.

### *Concerning the vessel in which Marcasite can be rightly sublimated. Chapter 47.*

Let us therefore collect that substance by its own method of sublimation, which is this: a very solid earthen vessel should be made, well-baked, to the length of half a man's height. As for the width, it should be such that a hand can enter within. And let its bottom be made so that it can be separated and joined, in the likeness of a single deep, flat dish.

The reason for the length of the vessel is so that a large portion of it may extend outside the fire and be cooled, so that the fumes of the sublimation <note>original: "sublimationis"; the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again in a purer form</note> may find a place of cooling and adhere to it, and not find a path for escape and their own loss. The reason for the glazing <note>original: "uitrificationis"; the application of a glass-like coating to seal the ceramic</note> of the vessel is so that the fumes rising in the place of their ascent do not find the wall of the aludel porous, and escaping, penetrate through it. The bottom of the aludel, however, is not glazed, because its bottom sits in the fire, which would melt its glazing; if that were melted, both the bottom and likewise the material to be sublimated would be melted and become glass. For it is the property of glass to conquer all things and convert them into itself.

Therefore, having considered all these things along with their causes, let a fire be made under the aludel until you are certain by true experience that the whole of it has ascended. The test, moreover, is the insertion of an earthen rod <note>original: "baculi terrei"; a ceramic testing tool</note>, well-baked, having a small hole in its head reaching to its middle, about the size of a pinky finger, near the very substance from which the sublimation is made. And if anything from the material to be sublimated adheres to the hole, it is not yet fully sublimated; if not, then it is sublimated. And by this same practice, you can be certain in all things to be sublimated. # FOURTH PART OF THE FIRST BOOK

to the same, and it follows one general order. Because whatever must necessarily be sublimated <note>Sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it turns into a vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify substances.</note> by fire should be done so without dregs, as these substances contain sufficient—even superfluous—dregs within themselves; the sign of this is the very difficulty of their sublimation. All bodies diminished from perfection <note>In alchemy, "imperfect" metals usually refer to base metals like lead, tin, copper, or iron, as opposed to "perfect" gold or silver.</note> are likewise sublimated in this same order. No diversity occurs in the method, except that the fire for sublimation is more intense for metals than it is for Magnesia, Marchesite, and Tutia <note>Tutia: zinc oxide; Marchesite: likely iron pyrites or a similar metallic mineral.</note>. Similarly, metals do not differ in their sublimations, except that some require the admixture of a substance to help lift them, while others do not, so that their elevation may be made easier.

However, one specific practical experience found in the sublimation of metals is useful: namely, that there should not be a large quantity of the body to be sublimated at the bottom of the aludel <note>Aludel: a pear-shaped chemical vessel used as a condenser in the sublimation process.</note>, because a great mass hinders the process. The bottom of the sublimation aludel should be flat, not concave, so that the body—spread thinly and evenly over the floor—can be elevated equally and fully in all its parts.

The metals that require the admixture of an elevating substance are Venus <note>Venus: the alchemical name for Copper.</note> and Mars <note>Mars: the alchemical name for Iron.</note>, because of the slowness of their melting. Thus, Venus requires Tutia, while Mars requires Arsenic; with these, they are easily elevated, since they agree most closely with them. Therefore, after considering these factors, let the sublimation be performed as with Tutia and similar substances, and let their sublimation be arranged in this same order with its specific causes and experiences.

-># THE HEIGHT OF PERFECTION BY GEBER<-

The reason for that invention <note>The "invention" refers to the *descensorium*, a specialized furnace or vessel used for downward filtration/distillation.</note> was threefold. First, so that when some material is enclosed in that vessel which is called the **descensory of Chemistry**, it may descend through its opening after it has melted, and by its descent, we may be certain that it has undergone fusion. The second reason is so that "weak" bodies <note>In alchemy, "weak" or "imperfect" bodies usually refer to base metals like lead or tin that oxidize or vaporize easily.</note> may be preserved from burning after they have been reduced from their **calxes** <term>calx: a powder produced by heating a metal; the oxide form</term>. For when we attempt to reduce weak bodies from their calxes, we cannot reduce every part of them at the same time. Therefore, if that part which was first reduced into a metallic body were to wait for the reduction of the whole, a greater quantity of it would vanish through the fire. It was necessary, therefore, to devise a way so that as soon as a part is reduced, it is removed from the fire. This is accomplished by the descensory. There is also a third reason for its invention: the **purification** of bodies from every foreign matter. For the melted body descends clean, and leaves every foreign thing behind in the cavity of the vessel.

Therefore, since the method of descent has been discovered for these three necessities, let its method be determined along with its instrument (previously described) and its purposes. We say, then, that its shape shall be such that its bottom is pointed, and its walls should end smoothly and equally at the sharpness of the bottom, so that each of the meltable substances can descend freely without sticking to the opening at the bottom. Its cover (if necessary) should be in the likeness of a flat **platter** <note>original: "parapsidis"</note> and should fit it well; and they should be made of good and firm earth <note>Refers to refractory clay that can withstand high heat.</note>, not easily cracking under the pressure of the fire.

Therefore, let the thing intended to be "descended" be placed into it, upon round sticks made of earth, so that they sit closer to the upper bottom; let it be covered, the joint secured, and placed in a fire of coals. Let it be blown upon until the entire substance descends into the vessel placed beneath it. However, if the substance is difficult to melt, it can be placed upon a flat board or one of small concavity, from which it can easily descend by tilting the head of the descensory once it has been melted.

Let us now speak, therefore, of the methods of all distillations, along with their causes. Of that which is done by ascent, there are two modes. One is performed with an earthenware pot filled with ashes <note>The "ash bath," providing even, high heat</note>. That which is done with ashes is performed with a greater, stronger, and sharper fire; however, that which is done with water uses a gentle and even fire. For water does not take on the sharpness of fire in the same way that ashes do. Therefore, through the method using ashes, colors and the thicker parts of the earth are usually raised. But with the method using water, it happens that the more subtle parts—those without color and approaching the nature of simple wateriness—are raised.

A more subtle separation is therefore achieved by the method performed with water than by that elicited with ashes. Experience has shown this to be true: for when one had distilled oil through ashes, he received the oil into the receiver scarcely altered. Wishing, however, to separate its parts, he was led by necessity to distill it through water. And then, through the repetition of this process, he separated the oil into its elemental parts, such that he extracted the whitest and clearest water from the deepest red oil, while the redness of that oil remained entirely in the bottom of the still. Bodies <note>original: "corpora"; in alchemy, this refers to solid metals</note> are treated differently than spirits <note>volatile substances like sulfur or mercury</note> or other things, and different bodies are likewise calcined in different ways. For soft bodies <note>referring here to lead and tin</note> have one general method for the purpose of **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of reducing a metal to a powder (oxide) through heat</term>, namely, that both can be **calcined** <term>calcined: burned to a powder</term> by fire alone, and by the sharpness of salt, whether both are similarly prepared or unprepared. 

The first method, therefore, by fire alone, is performed as follows: take an iron or earthen vessel shaped like a side-dish, the structure of which should be firm, and let it be fitted to a **calcination** furnace for these metals in such a way that coals can be thrown and blown under it. Then, let **lead** <term>plumbum</term> or **tin** <term>stannum</term> be thrown into the bottom of that vessel, which should sit firmly upon an iron tripod or three stone columns, and be similarly secured to the walls of its furnace by four or three stones wedging it against them, so that the vessel cannot be moved. 

The shape of the furnace should be the same as the form of the great ignition furnace, which has already been described and will be described again in a more complete discourse. Therefore, let a fire be lit in that furnace under the **calcination** vessel, powerful enough to melt the body being calcined. And when the body itself has created a black skin over it by the heat of the fire, let that be drawn away from it with an iron or stone shovel—one that does not allow itself to be burned, which would contaminate the **lime** <term>calx: the powdered remains of a metal after heating</term>. 

This **stripping** <term>exscoriatio: the removal of the oxidized surface layer</term> should be continued until the body itself is converted into powder. If it be **Saturn** <note>The alchemical name for lead</note>, let it be placed in a greater fire until its **lime** is changed into a very bright yellow color. But if it be **Jupiter** <note>The alchemical name for tin</note>, let it be similarly exposed and left until it is changed into a complete whiteness. 

In this, however, we make the craftsman careful: **Saturn** easily returns from its **lime** back into a metal body, but **Jupiter** does so with great difficulty. Therefore, lest he happen to err in the exposure of **Saturn** after its first pulverization to a greater fire, he must take care lest its **lime** return to a body before it is perfected. For everything deprived of its own proper moisture yields no fusion except that which leads to glass. Therefore, it is necessarily required that one hastens to reduce it quickly with a very swift impetus of fire. Otherwise, it is not reduced. Let the worker experiment with this, and he shall know.

The method of calcination for these two bodies <note>Tin and Lead</note>, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is as follows: a quantity of salt should be cast upon their surface, bit by bit, very frequently during their fusion. They should be mixed with much agitation using an iron rod over the fire, until through the mixture of salt they are turned into ash. Afterward, their lime is perfected through the same method of completion, with its proper considerations. But there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. For Saturn <term>Saturn: the alchemical name for Lead</term> is converted to powder more easily than Jupiter during the first labors of calcination; however, its lime is not perfected more easily than that of Jupiter. The cause of this depends on the fact that Saturn has a more fixed moisture than Jupiter.

# THE SUM OF PERFECTION BY GEBER. 87

The method for Venus <note>original: "Veneris"; refers to Copper</note> and Mars <note>original: "Martis"; refers to Iron</note> is the same, yet different from the first metals mentioned, and this is due to the difficulty of their melting. The method is that they should be beaten into thin plates and placed under strong ignition <note>intense heating without melting</note>, the intention of which is not to melt them. Because of the great amount of earthiness in them, and the large measure of burning and volatile sulfurousness, they are easily brought into a lime <note>original: "calcem"; a powdered metallic oxide</note> by this method. And this is because the proper continuity of the substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui"; Mercury, considered a primary building block of metals</note> is disturbed by the great amount of earthiness mixed within it.

Therefore, porosity is caused within them, through which the passing sulfurousness can fly away; and the fire, reaching it for that reason, can burn it and lift it away. Through this, therefore, it is left behind, and the parts become thinner and are converted into ash through the discontinuity of that thinness. The clear experience of this is that when a plate of Venus <note>Copper</note> is exposed to ignition, it will give off a sulfurous flame and cause a crushable scale to form on its surface. This is because the easier combustion of sulfur must necessarily occur from the parts closest to the surface.

The design of the furnace for this calcination is the same as the design for the distillation furnace, except that it ought to have only one large hole above its head, from which it may freely release the fumes. And the placement of the materials to be calcined should be in the middle of the furnace, so that they may receive the fire freely all around. Their vessel should be made of earth <note>clay or ceramic</note>, fashioned in the shape of a shallow bowl <note>original: "parapsidis"</note>.

The method for the calcination of spirits <note>volatile substances like sulfur or arsenic</note> is that, as they approach fixation <note>the state of being resistant to fire</note>, fire should be administered successively and little by little, increasing it so they do not flee, until it happens that they can tolerate the greatest fire. Their vessel should be round and closed on all sides, and the furnace the same as the one last mentioned.

With a similar furnace and a similar vessel, every thing is likewise calcined. However, we are excused from greater labor than that which is applied in guarding against flight <note>evaporation/sublimation</note>. Since other things...

Furthermore, a spirit that is merely purified preserves its nature better than one that is purified, fixed, calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note>, and dissolved. And therefore we prove through this, that all calcined substances <note>original: "calcinata"; materials reduced to powder by heat</note> approach the nature of salts or alums; therefore, it is necessary that they accompany one another in their properties. Truly, the method of solution <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid</note> is twofold: namely, by warm manure <note>original: "fimum"; used as a steady, gentle heat source in early chemistry</note> and by boiling water. Of these, there is one intention and one effect. The method by manure, therefore, is that the calcined material be placed in a glass flask <note>original: "ampullam uitream"</note>, and over it be poured a quantity of distilled vinegar <note>original: "aceti distillati"</note>, or something similar, twice its amount. Let its head be stopped up well so that it does not breathe <note>i.e., so that vapors do not escape</note>, and let it be left to dissolve under warm manure. Afterward, let the dissolved portion be removed by filter distillation. That which is not dissolved should be calcined again, and after calcination, let it be dissolved again in the same way, until through the reiteration of the work upon it, the whole is dissolved. Truly, the method which is done by boiling water is faster. It is thus: let the calcined material be arranged in a flask with vinegar in the same way, with the opening stopped so it does not breathe. This should be buried in a cauldron full of water and straw, as we have brought forth in order in the instructions for the method of distillation by water <note>referring to a "water bath" or bain-marie</note>. Afterward, let a fire be kindled under it until the water boils for an hour. After this, let the dissolved portion be distilled and kept aside. That which is not dissolved should be calcined again and dissolved again in the same order, until through reiteration the whole is dissolved.

of that coagulation <note>The process of turning a liquid or fluid substance into a solid state, a central goal in alchemy.</note>. Indeed, certain men have devised a method for that coagulation by keeping it in a tempered heat of fire. When they thought they had solidified it, they found that after its removal from the fire, it flowed just as before. Because of this, they were struck with amazement and wonder, vehemently arguing that this goal could not be reached. Others, however, assuming by necessity from natural principles that any moisture is converted into dryness by the heat of fire, attempted with persistent urgency to continue its preservation in the fire; and through this continuation, they reached a point where some of them converted it into a white stone, others into a red stone, and some into a yellow stone, which had neither the ability to melt nor to penetrate other metals. They were unable to determine the cause of these variations, and therefore they cast the work aside.

Others attempted to coagulate it with medicines <note>In this context, "medicines" refers to chemical elixirs or reagents added to a substance to change its properties.</note>, but they did not succeed; instead, they were deceived, either because they did not achieve solidification, or because the substance was imperceptibly thinned away, or because their coagulation did not take the form of any solid body. They remained ignorant of the cause of these differences. Others, composing artificial medicines, coagulated it by means of "projection" <note>The act of casting an alchemical agent upon a molten metal to effect transmutation.</note>, but their coagulation was not useful, since they converted it into an imperfect body. Likewise, they were unable to see the cause of this.

It is therefore expedient for us to explain the causes of these things, so that the craftsman may attain the mastery of that coagulation. As has already been sufficiently explained by us, the substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui" (living silver)</note> is uniform. For this reason, it is not possible to remove its wateriness in a short space of time by keeping it in the fire. Too much haste, therefore, was the cause of the first error. Furthermore, since it is of a subtle substance, it retreats from the fire. An excess of fire, therefore, is the cause of the error of those from whom it flees. It mixes easily with sulfur, arsenic, and marcasite <note>A term used historically for various metallic sulfides, often iron pyrites.</note>, because of their commonality in nature.

Truly, the fixation of marcasite <note>iron pyrites</note>, magnesia <note>likely manganese ore or a similar mineral</note>, and tutia <note>zinc oxide</note> is such that when, after their first sublimation, we have acquired what we want from them and cast away their dregs, we should repeat the sublimation upon them. This is done by repeatedly returning what ascended to the top back to what remained at the bottom for each of them, until they are fixed. The description of these vessels has already been provided.

### On Ceration. Chapter 55.

Ceration <term>Ceration: from the Latin "cera" (wax); the process of softening a hard substance until it flows like wax</term> is the softening of a hard, non-fusible thing to the point of liquefaction. From this, it is clear that the reason for this invention was so that a substance—which could not penetrate a body to alter it because it lacked the ability to melt—might be softened so that it flows and gains entry. Therefore, some have thought that ceration ought to be performed with liquid oils and waters. But that is erroneous, and entirely removed from the principles of this natural mastery, and rejected by the manifest works of nature. For we do not see that nature has placed a quickly-ending humidity in metallic bodies; rather, she has placed a long-lasting humidity for the necessity of their fusion and softening. For if she had placed such a [fleeting] humidity in them, it would necessarily follow that by a single ignition <note>heating to redness</note>, the bodies would happen to be totally deprived of moisture. Wherefore it would follow that after one ignition, any body could neither be hammered nor melted. For this reason, imitating the works of nature as much as we can, it is necessary for us to follow nature's method in cerating. Nature herself cerates at the root of the ceration of fusible things with a humidity that is above all other humidities, enduring the heat of the fire. Therefore, it is also necessary and expedient for us to cerate with a similar humidity. In no...

# FOURTH PART OF THE FIRST BOOK

However, this "waxy moisture" <note>original: "humiditas cerativa" — a substance's ability to melt like wax without evaporating</note> is found better, more feasibly, and more closely in some things than in others: namely, closely in sulfur and arsenic, but more closely and better still in quicksilver <note>mercury</note>. We see that the moisture of these substances does not leave their earthy base because of the strong union they achieved during nature's process of mixing. In all other things that possess moisture, however, you will find through experiment that the moisture is separated from its earthy substance during dissolution, and after that separation, the substance is deprived of all moisture. But in the aforementioned spirits <note>volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, and arsenic</note>, this does not happen. Therefore, there is no other means by which we can be excused from using them in the process of "waxing" <note>ceration: the process of softening a hard substance to a wax-like state</note>. The method of Waxing, therefore, is performed through them, by repeating their sublimation over the material to be softened so many times that, remaining within it with their moisture, they provide a good melting quality. This, however, will not happen before their perfect cleansing from every corrupting element. But it seems better to me that their oils should first be fixed by means of oil of tartar, and with those, every suitable and necessary waxing for this art should be performed.

### Preface dividing this second book into three parts. Chapter 56.

Now that the discussion of the principles of this mastery has been delivered, it is necessary—according to our promise—to pursue the intent of this art completely, in language appropriate to it. This consists of the consideration of every thing through which the perfection of this work may be more clearly shown. It also includes the consideration of the necessity of the perfection of the medicine <note>In alchemy, the "medicine" or "elixir" is the substance used to transform base metals into gold or silver.</note>; namely, that it should be discussed from which source that medicine may be more easily or more closely extracted for the complete perfection of everything imperfect. And similarly, it includes the consideration of the crafts <note>artificiorum</note> through which we may know whether the perfection is complete. Once these three things have been delivered, the entire knowledge of perfection will have been handed down, according to the needs of our art.

### *On the nature of Sulfur and Arsenic.* Chapter 58.

Therefore, asserting first the nature of the spirits, which are the principles of the bodies themselves—namely Sulfur, its companion <note>Likely referring to Arsenic, often paired with sulfur in alchemical theory.</note>, and Quicksilver <note>original: "argentum uiuum"; mercury.</note>. Thus, Sulfur and its companion possess a cause of corruption: an inflammable substance and earthy dregs. However, they possess a perfecting cause that lies midway between this and that. Similarly, the inflammable substance is a cause of corruption because it neither stands <note>remains stable under heat</note> nor causes other things to stand, and because it provides blackness to every kind of thing. Therefore, the cause of perfection in them is their moderate substance; because of its earthiness, it is not disturbed from penetration, which is perfected through good fusion. And because of its subtlety, its impression is not easily removed on account of flight <note>volatilization or evaporation</note>. However, their moderate substance is not a cause of perfection for bodies or for quicksilver unless it be fixed. For when it is not fixed, although its impression may not be removed easily...

It is never fixed <note>term: fixation (fixio) — the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate</note> unless it is calcined <note>term: calcination — heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or ash</note>, and once calcined, it yields no melting. That it cannot be fixed unless it is calcined is clear from the experiment of one who attempts to fix it without calcining; for he finds that it always flees <note>original: "fugere" — to evaporate or escape as vapor</note> until it is turned into earth. Its likeness is that of the nature of lime. 

However, this happens very little in the case of quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum" — mercury</note>, since it can be fixed without being turned into earth, and it can likewise be fixed with its conversion into earth. ### That a specific preparation must be applied to each of the imperfect bodies. Chapter 68.

From the discourses we have already recounted, it appears what remains superfluous or diminished from the works of nature in each of those which are imperfect bodies, according to their sufficient part. However, regarding the completion of what we omitted in the previous sections, we shall complete it here with sufficient discourse. 

First, therefore, since it happens that the changeable bodies of imperfection are of two kinds: namely, soft and low-melting <note>original: "ignibilia," referring to metals that melt easily at low heat</note>, such as Saturn <note>Lead</note> and Jupiter <note>Tin</note>; and those that are hard and not easily fusible, or fusible only with the application of intense fire <note>original: "ignitione"</note>, such as Mars <note>Iron</note> and Venus <note>Copper</note>—the former being non-fusible and the latter requiring intense heat—nature has necessarily taught us by informing us that, due to the diversity of their essences, we must administer different preparations at the root of their nature according to their requirements. 

There are, therefore, necessarily two bodies of one kind of imperfection to be transformed: namely, lead, which is called *melan* <note>original Greek: μέλαν</note>, that is, "black," and by the art is called Saturn; and the "shrieking" lead <note>referring to the "cry of tin" heard when bending the metal</note>, which is called *leukon* <note>original Greek: λευκὸν</note>, that is, "white." And in this opinion is Jupiter <note>Tin</note>. These are diverse from one another in the depths of their hidden parts, born from the root of their nature, and similarly in their manifest appearance. For Saturn is dark, livid, heavy, and black, and being without a shriek, it is totally mute. Jupiter, however, is white, slightly livid, but shrieks a great deal, and produces a ringing with a modest sound. 

We shall show you the difference in their depths, along with manifest experiments, arising from their necessary causes. From these, according to the "more or less," it befits the craftsman of a good mind to gather the order of preparation. First, therefore, let us narrate the preparation according to the order of the bodies; and afterwards, that of the coagulable quicksilver <note>Mercury</note> itself. But first, we deal with those of one kind—namely, the soft ones—and after this...

### *That the defect of imperfect metals must be supplied by medicine, but the superfluous must be removed by preparation. Chapter 69.*

The preparation of Saturn <note>Lead</note> is applied to its essence in many ways, and likewise for Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, according to the degree of their proximity to or distance from multiple perfection. Therefore, there is one type of corruption arriving from the depths of their innate root of nature—namely, the earthiness of the sulfurous quality and the impurity of the earth of quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, which are mixed into the essential nature of their principles of creation. There is another type of corruption coming upon them after their first mixing, bringing about decay; these are the burning sulfurous quality of the first kind, its impurity, and the foul substance of the quicksilver. All of these are things that corrupt the substance of the perfection of Saturn and Jupiter.

But of these two types, it is impossible for one to be removed by the medicine of any industry of the first order. The other, however, happens to be removed with a small amount of assistance. That which is impossible to remove occurs because these elements were mixed into the true essence within the principles of their own nature for this class of bodies, and they became the true essence itself. Therefore, since it is not possible to remove the true essence of any thing in nature while the thing itself remains, it was not possible to delete these corrupting factors from them. For this reason, certain Philosophers <note>Alchemists</note> thought that the Art <note>Alchemy</note> could not be achieved through this. But we, inquiring into this science in our own time, have arrived at this same conclusion, which also...

Similarly, by no method of ingenious preparation were we able to brighten the <term>bodies</term><note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to the base metals like lead, tin, copper, or iron.</note> with the fullness of their own bright luster without it happening that they were instead entirely stained and blackened. Because of this, we were likewise struck with amazement and for a long space of time lay hidden under the shadow of despair. Yet, returning to ourselves and tormenting ourselves with the immense afflictions of deep thought and meditation, we observed that the bodies diminished from perfection were, in the depths of their nature, foul, and nothing bright was to be found in them, since by nature it is not within them. For one cannot find in a thing that which is not there. Since, therefore, nothing of perfection is found in them, it necessarily follows that nothing superfluous is found in them either—neither in the separation of their diverse substances nor in the depths of their nature. And so, through this, we discovered that there was something diminished in them which must necessarily be completed by a material suitable to them that fulfills what is lacking. That which is diminished in them is, namely, a scarcity of <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: "argenti vivi" (living silver); mercury.</note> and its improper thickening. Therefore, the completion in them will be the multiplication of quicksilver, its proper thickening, and its permanent <term>fixation</term><note>The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note>. This, however, is perfected through a <term>medicine</term><note>The "Elixir" or "Philosopher's Stone" capable of curing the "sickness" of base metals.</note> created from that very substance. For since this medicine is brought into being from quicksilver, by the benefit of its clarity and splendor, it hides and covers their darkness by cloaking it; it draws out their splendor and converts it into brilliance. For when quicksilver, prepared as a medicine through our craftsmanship, has been cleansed and reduced into a most pure and shining substance, it will—when cast upon those things diminished from perfection—illuminate them and perfect them by its fixation. We shall describe this medicine in its own discourse. It follows necessarily from the preceding points that there are two necessary ways to find perfection: one through a material that separates the foul substance from the mixture, and the other through a medicine which [perfects] it.

### *On the preparation of Saturn and Jupiter. Chapter 70.*

Saturn and Jupiter are therefore prepared by manifold preparations according to the necessity of their approximation to greater perfection, namely by a common and a special mode of preparation. And it is done so that when the body has been calcined, then the water of alums or salts is poured over their lime, or glass is mixed with it, and it is reduced back into a body [metal]. This is then repeated upon these bodies in alternating turns until they show themselves completely clean. For since salts and alums and glass melt by a different fusion than the metals, they are therefore separated from them, and they carry the earthy substance away with them, leaving behind only the purity of the bodies. ## On the preparation of Mars. Chapter LXXII.

The preparation of Mars <note>Iron</note> is likewise manifold. For some is completed through sublimation, and some without sublimation. That which is done through sublimation is with arsenic, the method of which is this: let us contrive as deeply as we can to unite non-fixed arsenic to it, so that it may melt with it during fusion. There is also another preparation of Mars itself by means of arsenic, sublimed from it many times, until some quantity of the arsenic remains. For if this is reduced, there will emerge a white, fusible, and clean prepared substance. There is likewise a third method of its preparation through its fusion with lead and tutia.

From these things, indeed, flows that which is clean and white. ->*That the most perfect medicine must necessarily bring five different properties of perfection: namely, purity, color, fluidity, permanence, and weight; from which a conjecture may be formed as to what substances it should be drawn from.* Chapter 74.<-

Let us therefore first offer a universal discourse concerning medicines, along with their causes and manifest experiments. We suggest, therefore, that unless every superfluity is removed from the imperfect bodies—whether by the medicine or by the method of preparation—they will not be purified. Specifically, all superfluous sulfurousness <note>original: "sulphureitas"; the active, combustible principle in alchemy</note> and every unclean earthiness must be taken from them, so that they do not separate from the mixture during melting after the altering medicine has been cast upon them. When you have achieved this, you possess one of the hallmarks of perfection.

Similarly, unless the medicine also brightens and alters the body into a white or lemon-yellow color <note>original: "citrinum"; referring to the colors of silver and gold</note> according to the goal you seek—bringing a brilliance of luster and a clear beauty—the diminished bodies are not totally perfected by the process. Furthermore, unless it specifically brings about the fluidity of the Moon or the Sun <note>original: "Lunarem aut Solarem"; alchemical code for Silver and Gold</note>, the body is not alterable in its completion, because it does not remain stable during testing <note>original: "iudicijs"</note>, but separates entirely from the mixture and recedes. This point, determined more broadly by us in the following pages, is demonstrated in the chapter on the cupel <note>original: "cineritio"; a vessel used in the assaying of precious metals</note>. Furthermore, and unless...

If the medicine is not made permanent through a firm alteration of the impression <note>The "impression" refers to the alchemical influence or form being impressed upon the base metal</note>, its change is of no value, because the impression does not remain but vanishes. Furthermore, unless it brings the weights of perfection, it does not change the nature under a firm and true completion, in which there is no deception through the error of belief. For the weight of nature is one of the signs of perfection. It is clear, therefore, that since there are five differences of perfection, it is necessary for the medicine of our mastery <term>magisterium: the alchemical process or the "Great Work"</term> to bring these specific differences during the projection <note>The act of casting the elixir onto the molten base metal</note>. Through this, it is clear from what substances our medicine is drawn. For it is drawn from those things which are most closely joined to bodies, and which, as altering agents, adhere to them amicably in their depths. Therefore, while searching in other things, we have found in our discovery no other thing more than quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> to be befriended by the natures of bodies; by bestowing our work upon it, we find it to be the true medicine of alterable things in its completion, with a true and not insignificantly special alteration.

### On the preparations of the medicine to be applied, so that it may acquire the proper differences of properties. Chapter 75.

It remains, therefore, for us to describe its substance and the differences of the property of that substance in a determined way. And since we have not found it to change without the administration of its natural alteration, we have likewise found that it must necessarily be prepared, since it cannot be mixed in the depths without that method of preparation. That is to say, its substance must become such that it is mixed in the depths, even to the very core of the alterable body, without separation forever. This, however, does not happen unless it is greatly refined with the certain and determined preparation described in the chapter on sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the material</term>. And its impression likewise does not remain unless it is fixed; nor does it illuminate, unless the most brilliant substance is drawn from it.

-># SECOND PART OF THE SECOND BOOK<-

Because the greater the weight of the transformed bodies, the greater the perfection found in them through investigation by the art. Therefore, this useful discourse on medicines <note>In alchemical Latin, "medicina" refers to the agent of transformation or the "philosopher's stone" in its various stages, rather than a remedy for human illness.</note> is completed if we describe the differences between all medicines. We have indeed suggested that it is necessary for there to be a threefold difference in medicines. One is of the first order, another of the second, and another of the third.

I call a medicine of the first order any preparation of minerals which, when projected upon bodies diminished from perfection <note>Base metals like lead or tin, which the alchemist considers "sick" or "incomplete" versions of gold.</note>, impresses an alteration upon them; yet this does not bring about a sufficient completion, for it happens that the altered substance changes and is corrupted when the impression of that medicine totally evaporates. An example of this is every whitening sublimation of Venus <note>original: "Veneris" — Copper</note> or Mars <note>original: "Martis" — Iron</note> which has not undergone fixation. Of this kind is every addition of the color of the Sun <note>original: "Solis" — Gold</note> and Moon <note>original: "Lunae" — Silver</note>, or those mixed with Copper, placed over a cementing furnace, such as verdigris <term>ziniar: a green pigment or rust of copper used in alchemical coloring</term> and similar things. For this changes the metal with a mutation that does not last, but rather diminishes itself through exhalation.

We call a medicine of the second order every preparation which, when projected upon bodies diminished from perfection, alters them into some degree of completion, yet leaves behind some qualities of corruption entirely; such as the calcination <term>calcinatio: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or oxide</term> of bodies, by which everything fugitive <note>Volatile elements that evaporate easily</note> is deleted. In this category is the medicine that perpetually turns Silver yellow <note>To make it resemble gold</note>, or perpetually whitens Copper, while leaving other corrupt qualities within them.

Finally, I call a medicine of the third order every preparation which, when it reaches the bodies, removes all corruption by its projection, and perfects them with every quality of completion. This medicine is one and alone. And therefore, by it, we are excused from the labors of inventing the ten medicines of the second order. Thus, the work of the first order is called the "lesser"; that of the second is the "middle"; and that of the third is finally the "greater." This is the sufficient distinction of all medicines.
