Metals are generated from Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"; here referring to the philosophical principle of fluidity and metallic essence</note>, as is evident through the teachings of Aristotle and Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the influential Persian physician and philosopher</note>. Therefore, if these substances were to become metals, it would be necessary for them first to pass into the "prime matter" <term>materia prima: the formless base substance from which all things are created</term> of metals. But because this cannot be done by artificial means, these lesser substances will by no means become metals. Thus, the second part of the preceding argument is sufficiently clear, as was declared in the previous chapter.

Secondly, regarding the same point: Because the "lesser minerals"—which are the starting point of the art—cannot be artificially transformed into Mercury (the beginning), they likewise do not reach the middle or the end, which are metal and the tincture <term>tinctura: the "philosopher's stone" or elixir capable of transmuting metals</term>. This logic holds true because nourishment in a human being cannot become a human through generation unless it is first converted into sperm; only then, by adding its like, is a new human generated. 

But because the lesser minerals are of a nature foreign to metals—even though they participate in some mineral power—they are nevertheless of a weaker virtue and are prone to burning <note>original: "adustibilia"; meaning they are consumed by fire rather than refined by it</note>. Therefore, the metallic nature does not delight in them, but rejects them. Nature preserves those things which are of its own kind. For example: if water and earth were mixed, they would then separate from one another, because earth seeks the bottom since it is heavy and dry, while water seeks the surface. And in no way can they be joined artificially so that these two natures remain united as one nature, even though water can wash and cleanse the earth. But that the dryness of earth could be artificially changed into the watery moisture of water is believed to be impossible, even if the earth is soaked by the water. 

In the same way, lesser minerals can be joined with metals to purge them, and in some way introduce a new form; but nature does not allow them to remain permanently with the metals, nor to ripen that which is immature. Therefore, those people are fools who introduce so many and such diverse dealings and sophistries <note>deceptive or fraudulent practices</note> to deceive men. Namely, they use disproportionate things which neither give nature its due nor receive it: such as afterbirth, eggshells, hair, the blood of a red-haired man, the basilisk <note>a mythical serpent; here likely a coded or literal reference to toxic ingredients</note>, quicksilver of vines, herbs, human dung, and an infinite variety of dungs. That the transforming agent converts the thing to be changed into its own nature is proven because every natural generator generates its own likeness; but because the generating nature of the four spirits is earthy, it will therefore generate its own likeness, which will also be earthy matter just like itself. ### On the difference between common sulfur and the simple, non-burning sulfur of the philosophers. Chapter XI.

Now we must inquire concerning the difference between the simple, non-burning sulfur of the philosophers and common sulfur. Since the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or Geber, often cited simply as "The Philosopher" in alchemical texts.</note> speaks generally: *Sulfur coagulates Mercury* <note>original: "Sulphur coagulat Mercurium"</note>, does every sulfur coagulate Mercury? ### How white and red sulphur exist in the Moon and the Sun. Chapter XII.

Since it has been said that the red sulphur of the philosophers exists in the Sun <note>The Sun represents Gold in alchemical symbolism</note> through greater digestion, and white sulphur exists in the Moon <note>The Moon represents Silver</note> through lesser digestion. Also, the philosopher says that each of the perfect bodies already actually contains its own good sulphur with Mercury: namely, gold contains golden sulphur, and silver contains silvery sulphur. Whence it is asked: Whether any foreign things can cause this in the bodies? Since art, with nature mediating, is nothing but the cooking and digestion of that nature through simple labor. I say no. Because it was said previously that in them there is no matter of greater temperance or of less dross than in these two bodies <note>Gold and Silver</note>.

### That there are only two particulars that are true in this art, the first of which is in Mercury. Chapter XV.

First, I declare universally to all observers to whom these presents may come, that in the entire sequence of this art, there are only two particulars <note>In alchemy, a "particular" refers to a specific process or substance that works on a limited scale, as opposed to the "universal" elixir.</note> which are particularly perfected according to the philosophers and nature. This is despite the fact that deceivers create infinite sophistications, whitenings, and reddenings, by which the faithful are deluded. The first particular, both in the white <note>The stage of making silver.</note> and in the red <note>The stage of making gold.</note>, exists in Mercury, without the administration of the "perfect medicine," although the body with which it is perfected contains within itself its own tincture <note>A substance capable of changing the color and quality of a metal.</note> in a particular way, if it is moved by art and operation as nature requires. The first thing that is particularly perfected in nature from either species is this: since Mercury is the first matter of all metals, composed of a very sulfurous white earth and clear water—and therefore the whiteness of the earth shines through the clarity of the water, and the color in it is a most brilliant white, as experience teaches—and since it is immature, it is possible for the Sun <note>Gold</note> and Moon <note>Silver</note> to be made from it. Whence the philosopher says: Let it be mixed with other metallic bodies, because they are of its own matter, and they themselves were generated from it; and therefore, through that artifice, one can transmit a digested nature into it, so that it may be perfected with them. And thus, it becomes like the metals with which it is embraced, without any foreign admixture, since nature simply rejoices in its own nature, and not through any other foreign medium—namely, with the Sun it becomes Gold, with the Moon it becomes Silver, with Venus it becomes Copper, and so with the others. Through putrefaction <note>original: "putrefactio"; in alchemy, this refers to the breaking down or "death" of a substance to allow for its rebirth</note>, the dissolution and separation of all things bound together in nature occurs. Thus, the parts that were bound to one another are separated, so that each part is set apart from the others. This happens through the loosening of the elements which were joined together in the generation of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"; here referring to the philosophical or "living" mercury, the essential spirit of metals</note>, namely water and earth. When these same parts have been purified in their nature through conversion, they are joined together again; and because of their cleansing, they love one another more than they did before. However, this separation cannot occur in physical bodies except through the spirit. In this way, art <note>meaning the "Art" of Alchemy</note> transcends nature in one respect: that artificial things are made suddenly, whereas natural things were previously made over a long duration.

Do not believe that these are common elements, such as water from a cloud and the like; rather, the "water" is the moist quality, "earth" is the cold, "air" is the warm, and "fire" is the dry. These exist within the natures of composed things. Since art can by no means separate parts so naturally that they are simply transformed back into the elements exactly as they were before, nature first changed one quality into another. In such a way, art can indeed separate them, so that the moist is separated from the dry, and the cold from the warm. 

Yet, one quality still possesses the nature of another in some part due to their natural mixing; because of this, they can be joined back together by art just as they were divided. For if one quality did not share in the nature of another—namely, water sharing the nature of earth in its coldness, and air sharing the nature of water in its moisture, and so on for the rest—then it would follow that the natural work would be totally destroyed. The elements would then be "simple" <note>meaning pure, unmixed elements</note>, just as they were before the generation of Mercury. Art would have destroyed nature by starting from the head—namely from Gold and silver—and going back to the first thing, which is Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum uiuum"; literal mercury</note>, and even beyond these principles to the simple elements as they were before Mercury's generation. This, however, is impossible to achieve so remotely through art. And if it were possible, it would then follow that from the beginning, outside of the first matter—namely the Mercury of metals,

### Concerning partial deceptions. Chapter XVII.

Aristotle <note>The author cites Aristotle, though this specific quote likely comes from the "De Mineralibus," a text attributed to him in the Middle Ages but actually written by Avicenna</note> says: Let the practitioners of Alchemy know that the species of things cannot be truly transmuted, but they can make things similar to them, such as tinting a red substance with yellow so that it appears to be gold, and tinting a white substance until it is very similar to gold or silver. ### Concerning the universal way, a general discourse. Chapter XVIII.

Having concluded the prologue of this art and its particular applications, we shall now speak of the universal way, in which art imitates nature. Now, the universal way—as you have heard above—is possible within the nature of metals: to plant branches upon which grow flowers of wonderful scent and little roses, both white and red. The first step in beginning, however, is to dissolve the stone into its first matter; this is the conjunction of body and spirit, so that from them one Mercurial water <note>original: "aqua Mercurialis"</note> may be made. Whence Avicenna <note>An influential Persian physician and philosopher (c. 980–1037) often cited in Western alchemy.</note> says: "The first step in beginning is to dissolve the stone into its own Mercury." Whence Rhazes <note>original: "Rasis"; refers to the Persian polymath Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925).</note> the philosopher says: "Unless you dissolve the bodies, you labor in vain." That is: Silver and Mercury for the white elixir, and Gold and Mercury for the red elixir. And this is done in a dew-bath <note>original: "balneo rorido"; a gentle steam or vapor bath</note> for the purpose of putrefaction, so that the bodies may be dissolved by the viscosity of the Mercurial water. Whence Parmenides <note>An ancient Greek philosopher; here cited as an alchemical authority.</note> says:

# THE WRITINGS OF RICHARD THE ENGLISHMAN

When the permanent water is joined into one with that which was with it from the beginning, there follows the division of the elements and their purification. Whence Albertus Magnus <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a renowned scholar and patron saint of scientists who was often cited in alchemical texts</note> says: "Four are made from one, and four are one": that is, from the Mercurial water <note>original: "aqua Mercuriali"; in alchemy, this refers to the "philosophical mercury," the essential fluid or life-force of matter</note>. The third step is the cleansing of the earth, of which the philosopher Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: "When this water putrefies with its earth, the entire mastery <term>mastery: the successful completion of the alchemical process</term> will be directed by this." Whence the philosopher Rasis <note>Rhazes (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and alchemist</note> says: "Join the dry with the moist; the moist is water, but the dry is earth."

Afterward follows the sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again, used here to purify the spirit</term> of the earth, of which the philosopher Parmenides says: "Sublime that which has been whitened with a swift fire, so that the spirit which you find within it may depart from it, and the earth may remain calcined <note>reduced to a powder by heat</note>." Regarding this earth, the philosophers Parmenides and Morienus say: "Do not despise the ash which is at the bottom, for it is the crown of your body, and the ash of permanent things." Thus the four elements are prepared, as you have understood above.

Do not join them before their cleansing, since they would separate on account of their impurity; as Ascanius says: "Spirits are not joined to the body until they have been perfectly stripped of their impurities." And the white and red ferment <note>substances added to "leaven" or transform the base metal into silver (white) or gold (red)</note> are joined according to whether the elements are white or red. If white, then fire is required. If red, then the elements are turned red through fire, so that it may digest, mature, solidify, and absorb the filth of the waters in the conjunction.

Let it possess the proportional virtues of the four elements: of earth in coldness and dryness, of water in coldness and moisture, of air in moisture and heat, and of fire in heat and dryness. Fire and earth are the extreme elements. Water and air are the middle elements, which you must join through due and true weights, so that they may love each other more than before. First, join the earth with the water. Second, join the air with the fire. And thus convert the natures, and you shall find what you seek. Then the earth is fit for dissolving, the water effective for cleansing, the oil or air in which the spirit is carried is for mixing, and the fire is for tinting <note>original: "tingendum"; the final stage of coloring the metal to its new form</note>. Thus the body retains the spirit just as the spirit retains the soul, with the addition of the ferment.

The author of the book which is called the Rosary says: I descended into my garden so that I might see the plants of various things springing forth, and among the other flowers of my Rose Garden, I came upon a snowy or white rose, and likewise one decorated with a bloody or red hue. # THE ROSARY

<note>original: ROSARIVS</note>

envious. The first type composes deceptive books, testifying to their own frauds and sophistry, and they write the titles of good philosophers at the head of their chapters so that they might appear to possess the true art and the perfect elixir <note>The "elixir" was the sought-after substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or curing all diseases</note>. And so that they may be more believed by men, they carry powders of stones, either white or red, and they handle gold and silver; but those who follow them fail in their works when they put those writings to the test. 

The second type is entirely envious, and has composed books concerning those things which are furthest removed from the truth, in order to distance men from the true path as much as he can. He strives to prove his sayings through mere logic, which to the foolish seem most certain. He places the art in herbs, and the fruits of plants, and in many strange and distant vegetables. Or, so that he may seem to leave us the true art, he speaks more philosophically by taking his foundation from the four elements—which are the philosophical materials—and he extracts them from many things, such as from vegetables, animals, and many other strange sources: namely from eggs, hair, blood, dung, urine, semen, toads, and many others, just as their writings demonstrate and declare. 

Or he substitutes one thing for another, either metaphorically or plainly, and places the whole art either in the aforementioned principles or in distant "middle minerals" <term>middle minerals: substances that were categorized between metals and earths, often used as reagents</term>, such as vitriol <note>original: atramentum</note>, borax salt, alum, marcasite, magnesia, tutia <note>zinc oxide</note>, and many other minerals. And although the aforementioned things sometimes assist in speeding the process, or in cleansing, or in the intensification of color, nevertheless those who present them as the complete philosophical material are envious. And thus they reveal the art, or even cover it up, and seduce the foolish so that they might despise the art; or even if they take the true material and mineral nature, nevertheless through their various fictional, impossible, or inept operations, they prevent the foolish from reaching completion. And oh, you novice Alchemists...

# THE FIRST CHAPTER.

*The promise and division of the things to be said concerning the operations of Alchemy. Section I.*

In the first chapter, I shall speak of all the operations which proceed from the matter with divine aid, and so forth. No sophisticated <note>In this context, "sophistic" refers to fraudulent or "fake" alchemy intended to deceive rather than achieve true transmutation.</note> deception shall enter this book; I will always set down the regimen that leads to perfection. Indeed, there are many things that assist the work. I say briefly that the aid for calcination <note>The process of reducing a metal to a powder or "ash" through heat or chemical action.</note> is this (and first I shall speak of the bodies):

*Concerning the Calcination of Saturn and Jupiter. Section II.*

Saturn <note>The alchemical name for Lead.</note> and Jupiter <note>The alchemical name for Tin.</note> are calcined first with the help of fire and the skill of the craftsman; this is done with a fire that does not exceed their point of fixation, in a strong earthen vessel, stirring with an iron rod until they are turned to ash. These ashes are then soaked with sharp, cleansing waters. For the red color, purified human urine, "water of blood," or red vinegar is effective. For the white color, white vinegar, common salt water, alum water, and many other bitter substances are useful. After soaking, the material is dried by the fire or the Sun until it reaches the state of a white or red lime <note>original: "calcem"</note>. Likewise, they are calcined with the help of salts, and that calcination is good; also through the help of vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid or a sulfate mineral.</note> and other sharp substances. They are also calcined with the aid of sulfur or orpiment <note>original: "auripigmenti"; a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, and that method is better. But they are best calcined with Mercury <note>Quicksilver.</note> in this manner: First, let them be amalgamated, ground, and washed with sharp liquids until they are perfectly cleansed; then let them be mixed with sharp salts by grinding, and with alums and other bitter things; let them be dried and eroded, and then the falseness <note>Impurities or non-metallic dross.</note> is removed by washing. However, before it is dried, let the Mercury be extracted with salt through sublimation, and so there remains...

A white powder <note>original: "calx alba"; literally 'lime,' referring to the oxide powder resulting from heating a metal</note> remains, than which none can be better. And I give you a general rule: that in whatever way Jupiter <note>the alchemical name for Tin</note> is calcined with fire, it produces a white powder; Saturn <note>the alchemical name for Lead</note> always produces a red one, unless it has been whitened with sharp substances <note>acidic or corrosive liquids like vinegar</note>.

### On the calcination of Venus and Mars. § III.

Venus <note>Copper</note> and Mars <note>Iron</note> are calcined with the aid of fire. First, in a reverberatory furnace <note>a furnace that reflects heat onto the material</note>, if their filings are placed inside, they are calcined by the reflection of the flame. From Mars is made "Saffron of Iron" <note>original: "crocus ferri"; iron oxide</note>, which is called the cement of iron. From Venus is made simple "burnt copper" <note>original: "aes ustum"</note>, or *chalkos kekaumenos* <note>original: "χαλκος κεκαυμενος"; Greek for burnt copper</note>. They are also calcined by heating them to a glow and quenching them in sharp liquids until they are totally converted into scales. Just as Jupiter and Saturn are calcined by the removal of their dross <note>scoria</note>, the powder is then soaked with sharp and salty liquids until it becomes red and clean. The powder of Venus and Mars can also be whitened. They are also calcined with sulfur and orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide</note> mixed with plates or filings of the metals, or even with salts, alums, and other corrosive substances. The powder is then prepared by washing and drying until it is as desired. They are also calcined very well by heating and quenching in Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>; whatever can be scraped off with a knife during each quenching is removed, and the work is repeated until it is finished. It is then prepared by washing and drying with salts and by drawing off the Mercury, and it will become an excellent powder. And know that the powder of a "body" <note>a metal</note> is not fixed unless it is calcined with fire. I say this because all bodies can be calcined over the vapors of sharp liquids, or with the liquids themselves. However, the best calcination of the bodies is done with Mercury.

### *On the calcination of other things and mixtures. Section 5.*

Many other things are also calcined in order to extract the tincture <note>Tincture: the essential soul or coloring principle of a substance capable of transforming metals.</note> from them, and so that their parts may be refined and cleansed. ### *On the sublimation of spirits. Section 6.*

Both spirits and mineral intermediaries <note>Intermediaries: substances like salts or vitriols that sit between "spirits" and "bodies" (metals).</note> are sublimated with assistance. Spirits are sublimated either by salts, or by vitriols <note>original: "atramentis"; refers to sulfate minerals used as reagents.</note>, or by alums, or by bodies <note>Metals.</note>, or by a mixture of these. And note, that sublimation is performed for the sake of purifying the tincture. If spirits are sublimated with impure things, they become fouled. If they are sublimated with things that cling to them, they remain more fixed with the tincture below, which is what we seek. Therefore, it is necessary that they first be cleansed by sharp substances <note>Acids or corrosive salts.</note> and by washing, or by a single separation of the impure from the pure. Think diligently upon this. For that medium is a secret. Sublimate the cleansed spirits with the pure limes of the bodies until they are fixed, and you will see that I have spoken the truth.

For that which is excessively volatile, along with the impure earthiness, are separated by sublimation, and there remains a tempered substance, as I have said, which is what we seek. They are also sublimated with elevating things, such as sulfur, orpiment <note>A deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, Mercury, and other

### On the sublimation of the perfect bodies. §. VIII.

### On fixation. §. IX.

Furthermore, every volatile thing is fixed when it is cleansed by the aid of fire, namely by daily decoction <note>prolonged heating</note>, and this is my secret; or by the help of some fixed thing, that is, through imbibition <note>soaking</note> and the repetition of the aforementioned things, as I have described clearly enough regarding sublimation. And this is one of my great secrets. Bodies are also fixed, as I have prefigured, by calcining <note>reducing to powder by heat</note> or by cooking with fire alone.

### On distillation. §. X.

Moreover, many things are distilled for the assistance of this work. Water is distilled from green or Roman Vitriol <note>iron or copper sulfates</note>, from saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note>, and from feathery alum <note>likely asbestos or a specific form of aluminum sulfate</note>, which is of the greatest value for the aid of this work; for with this water, all bodies are marvelously dissolved.

### Concerning the particulars for the white work in general. Section 14.

Behold, I have described to you all the true and necessary operations in the work of this art to shorten the labor and to assist nature in a general sense. Now, to satisfy your requirements, I will explain the better special and particular methods in this chapter. First, therefore, how the bodies <note>The "bodies" refer to the metals, such as gold and silver.</note> are augmented, and afterwards concerning the shortening of time and labor, and the elixir. And because the true red <note>The "red" refers to the goal of making gold.</note> can in no way be made unless the white <note>The "white" refers to the goal of making silver.</note> precedes it, I give to you such things for augmenting the "white roses" <note>A poetic term for the silver-making process.</note> so that perfect Moon <term>Luna: the alchemical name for silver</term> may be made. 

First, the body of the Moon must be dried, and this is done through the calcination <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term> which I have described. And this is the reason: so that the moisture of that substance with which we propose to augment it may adhere to it more radically and firmly without separation. Then, the other non-fixed body <note>A "non-fixed" body refers to a volatile metal or mineral, like mercury or antimony, that evaporates when heated.</note> with which you propose to work must be calcined, and this is so that it may be fixed by the other. For the volatile element in them flies away through the calcination of the fire, and there remains a pure and unleavened earth. Through this same calcination, the sticky oiliness and impurity are deleted from the body, and it is reduced to its original state, and there remains a clean earth, neither burning nor blackening the bodies. 

Then, dissolve the lime <note>The powder resulting from calcination.</note> of the Moon into clean and clear water, just as I demonstrated to you in the section on Dissolution. Secondly, likewise dissolve the unleavened lime of whichever body you choose; join the waters, and freeze <note>In alchemy, "congelation" or freezing often refers to the solidification of a liquid into a solid mass.</note> that well-mixed solution into a white mass, and at the end of the freezing, descend through the *botum* <note>original: "botum"; likely referring to a specific type of alchemical vessel or a crucible with a perforated bottom for filtration.</note>. And this is the best method that I have ever tested: I took one part of the fixed body and three parts of the non-fixed. Likewise, I joined the dissolved lime of the Moon and the water of the non-fixed body; I joined this water again, and I placed the joined mixture with the first aforementioned mass, which had been again calcined and dissolved, and

->Let us proceed to the augmentation of red roses.<-

The first general rule is this: in every red work, place <term>Sun</term> <note>original: "Solem"; refers to Gold</note>, just as you placed <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "Lunam"; refers to Silver</note> in the <term>unleavened work</term> <note>original: "azymo"; likely referring to the pure white stage of the stone</note>. Those which are reddened are these: the calx of <term>Mars</term> <note>Iron</note>, <term>Venus</term> <note>Copper</note>, and <term>Saturn</term> <note>Lead</note>. However, the calx of the Moon, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>Tin</note>, and fixed <term>Mercury</term> <note>Quicksilver</note> are not reddened by the aid of fire alone in this first chapter.

Behold the treasure of the philosophers! Nevertheless, in this first chapter, they are reddened with coloring agents, such as <term>sulfur</term>, <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "atramentum"; a sulfate mineral used for dyes and inks</note>, iron-water, and the red "philosophical oil" extracted from minerals, vegetables, or animals.

Once they are reddened through that same calcination in corrosive or dissolving waters—I mean the more reddish ones—join the waters, congeal them, and let them descend into a red mass, just as you did with the white. Repeat this work fifteen times, as you did with the unleavened work, and you will have a perfect operation. 

For in this work, you can observe every method of operating that I described in the white work; and this applies to those things which can be reddened with the aid of fire. It remains for us to declare here that all calxes of bodies can be reddened with the assistance of many coloring things. But because so many good and true things regarding such matters are found in the philosophical books of this art—concerning waters that tint with redness, powders, and oils with which calxes are so often soaked, dried, dissolved, congealed, and brought down unto redness—it therefore seems superfluous to us to treat of them. However, you may receive from me a special <term>tincture</term> <note>A concentrated substance capable of transforming or coloring metals</note> of the Sun, for your satisfaction.

### A specific procedure for the red color. §. XVII.

Wash iron filings <note>original: "limaturam Martis," literally filings of Mars, the alchemical name for iron</note> in hot salt water, then in hot fresh water, and finally many times—perhaps twenty times—in vinegar, until the filings are clear and very clean. Place them in a glass or glazed vessel with the best white vinegar for several days, until they turn deeply red through this process, which will happen quickly. Then, place the whole mixture into a glass distilling vessel and distill it repeatedly until those filings totally disappear. For they will undoubtedly be sublimated <note>converted into vapor and then solidified</note> with the aforementioned vinegar, and all those filings will pass over into a red water. Let this water sit undisturbed for several days. This water wonderfully tints prepared and molten silver <note>original: "Lunam," literally Moon, the alchemical name for silver</note> into a red color. In every repetition of the work, moisten the metal oxides <note>original: "calces"</note> with this water, dry them, dissolve, congeal, and let them flow down <note>original: "descende," likely referring to the process of filtration or liquification</note> until the tincture is sufficient. This water is considered mineral and corporeal in nature.

Another good tincture is made in this manner: Take one pound of egg yolks, one pound of fresh human blood, and two pounds of well-cleaned human hair. Mix these together in a round glazed vessel. Next, take two pounds of well-ground sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note> and mix everything together. Place the glazed vessel in a bed of sifted ash and light a gentle fire beneath it. When everything has been dissolved into a liquid, cast upon it an amount of yellow sulfur equal to half the weight of all the other medicines. Quickly remove the vessel from the fire, stirring everything together. Afterward, cast the whole mixture into a gourd-shaped vessel <note>original: "cucurbitam"</note> for distilling. Distill it over the dregs repeatedly, mixing the dregs with the water that distills from them, until everything remaining in the bottom is dry. This mixture, when ground and congealed with dissolved metal oxides, tints remarkably. This water is a vegetable or animal tincture.

## CHAPTER TWO

### *That Mercury alone is the cause of perfection. Section 1.*

It was stated above that the final intention of this most precious art is to improve imperfect metals and lead them to the highest degree. Their imperfection and corruption proceed from a lack of good and pure fixed quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi fixi"; quicksilver is the traditional name for mercury</note>, as I have said many times, and as all skilled philosophers say. It follows, therefore, that it alone is the perfecting agent. Let us therefore choose it and perfect it, just as the philosophers who possessed perfection did in their time. Whatever is written, it alone is the stone which philosophers praise everywhere, which they hide in infinite parables, fictitious writings, and metaphors, and which they reveal through their great philosophies. And now, by the grace of God, the Spirit has inspired me such that with two of its words, I shall explain all the philosophical books concerning this art. Behold the word of the Holy Spirit: MERCURY IS THE STONE WHICH PHILOSOPHERS HONOR. My heart is divided <note>likely meaning "opened" or "poured out" in revelation</note>, and like an opening book, let anyone read and pay attention. We seek quicksilver alone. For in it is everything that we desire; therefore, it contains its own tincture <note>a "tincture" in alchemy is the substance capable of transforming or coloring metals into gold</note> within itself. Oh, what a precious and delightful creature that is! For God created nothing better, except for the rational soul. It has within itself body, soul, and spirit. The body stands firm, the soul gives life, and the spirit tints <note>or "tinges," referring to the power of transmutation</note>. These are in mercury alone, congealed from the thickness of water by the power of pure, non-burning sulfur. Mercury, therefore, is our stone, nor can it be any other thing, which we call "dry water" because it is uniformly thickened by the power of unleavened <note>original: "azymi"; meaning pure or unmixed</note> or red sulfur,

->On the difference between Mercuries. §. II.<-

But I tell you this: that Quicksilver made from Gold is incomparably of greater virtue, and gives a swifter fixation <note>the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note> than that which was not previously a metal body; yet it is always Quicksilver from Quicksilver, and it is hot and moist, and masculine. ->A comparison suggesting the universal way. §. III.<-

Do not all things that are born, or plants that have come forth from the earth, always return to the earth? And after these have been in that same earth and have rotted over time, then the whole is earth. But consider what virtue that earth possesses. For we see that grain is born from the earth, having a stalk and many seeds; and if the stalks are then artificially put back into the earth when they have become manure, we see that all the manure returns into earth through rot <note>original: "putrefactionem," a key alchemical stage of breaking down matter</note>. But if the reserved seeds are placed again in that same earth of their aforementioned stalks, they are increased much more, as is well known to experienced farmers. So it is that bodies submerged in Mercury return through suitable rot into the Quicksilver which they were before; and afterwards, the metallic seeds, cast into that same rotted earth, are multiplied and grow beyond measure.

### Practice Veiled in Darkness. Section IIII.

The method of acting is truly according to nature. Our quicksilver <note>Latin: *Argentum vivum*; common mercury</note>, congealed or thickened by the power of unleavened or red non-burning sulfur, must first be cleansed of all filth and superfluity that can be removed by ingenuity. That ingenuity is sublimation, which is done as follows: Let the stone be placed in an open vessel over a moderate fire, stirring the Mercury itself so that all the superfluous humidity—which is accidental to it and by which the work would be corrupted—may fly away. Do not omit this step. Then, after all the watery and undigested matter (which was too volatile) has been cast off by a fire that does not overcome its radical fixation, there will remain a substance tempered between the fixed and the non-fixed, fit for completing this work.

And let there be a seed or ferment most purely cleansed, of which one part suffices for twelve parts of the cleansed stone. Let an ingenious amalgamation <note>The process of mixing mercury with another metal to form a paste</note> of both be made. Then, let the whole amalgam be placed in a very strong glass vessel with a narrow neck, or in an earthen one capable of sustaining the density or compaction of glass (which is better), and let the mouth be firmly sealed.

Let a large and thick philosophical furnace be made, in the middle of which is placed a very strong, ample earthen vessel capable of enduring the fire. In that vessel, all the containers holding the matter are to be placed. Then let the furnace be covered and closed at the top with a thick lid. Let there be three or four holes in its summit to direct the smoke away, and let a slow fire be applied perseveringly. A "slow fire" is defined as one that cannot overcome the fixation of the stone; the rule of the fire ought to be such that lead would remain continually molten within it. And this alone I manifest. For by such a regimen, you will have completed putrefaction <note>The stage of decomposition, often associated with the color black</note> in one hundred and twenty-four days. Blackness is the approved sign of putrefaction. Furthermore, by the aforesaid regimen, you will have the second sign, which will be a lasting redness...

Indeed, in the proportionate mixing of the aforementioned prepared things, a new form results, and thus the elixir is made, insofar as the matter is more digested and colored than the natural Sun <note>gold</note>.

...he then applied himself and labored in the work of the mastery <note>The "mastery" or *magisterium* refers to the successful completion of the alchemical process to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, whereby its composition weighed heavily upon him; he doubted it in many ways and was likewise ignorant of the natures of the composition of things. The first of these is the craft of washing, which they call the "cleansing of the bodies." <note>In alchemy, "bodies" usually refers to the seven base metals.</note> The other is indeed to make gold from living mercury <note>original: "azot uiuo." These four masteries and crafts were explained by the wise in their books concerning the composition of this Great Work. Therefore, in this book of mine, I shall describe the operation itself and its completion.

Whoever reads this book of mine should also read something of geometry and learn its measurements, so that he may correctly construct the furnaces <note>original: "clibanorum"</note> and not exceed their proper proportions through either increase or decrease. He must also know the quantity of the fires and the method or even the degree of the vessel used in the work. Similarly, he should see and understand what the innermost root and principle of the mastery is; it is to the work what the womb is to animals, in which they are generated and receive both their creation and nourishment, as was said before. 

Unless the matter of the mastery finds a suitable vessel for itself, the deed and its work will be destroyed, and its practitioners will not find what they seek. The matter itself will not proceed to the effect of generation because, when it fails to find the cause of generation—the root and the proper heat—a failure of destruction will occur in the operations. This same thing happens regarding the quantity of weights: when the weights are unsuitable in the compound <note>original: "composito"</note>, with parts of that same nature exceeding their limits through increase or decrease, the specific property of the compound is destroyed, and the effect of the compound becomes hollow and void. 

I will show you one example: Do you not see that in soap, with which clothes are washed, cleansed, and made white, this property is generated through its correct composition, because of the equality, the right proportions, and the due balance...

It is not dissolved, except through the congealing of the spirit. Both the body and the soul, when they are joined together, each acts upon its partner, making it similar to itself. An example of this is water and earth; for when water is joined to earth, it strives to dissolve the earth with its humidity, and with its power and properties which are within it, making the earth more subtle <note>In alchemy, "subtle" refers to a substance being refined, purified, or made less dense</note> than it was before, and rendering the earth similar to itself, for water was more subtle than earth. In the same way, the soul acts upon the body. Likewise, the water is thickened by the earth and becomes similar to the earth in density, because earth is thicker than water. 

And you should know that between the dissolution of the body and the congealing of the spirit, there is no difference in time, nor is there a separate process, such that one could exist without the other. Just as there is no separate span of time between water and earth in their joining—where one could be distinguished or separated from the other in their operations—rather, they have one limit, one deed, and one and the same operation revolves around the two of them simultaneously, before the composition. 

I have said "before the composition" so that whoever reads this book and hears of "dissolution" and "congealing" as I have described them, does not think this is the "composition" named by the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the ancient alchemical authorities like Hermes Trismegistus or Geber</note>; for if he thought so, he would be in error regarding his work and his knowledge. Their union and their suffering <note>original: "passio"; in this context, it refers to the chemical reaction or undergoing of change</note> occurs over the fire. 

For heat is its nourishment, and the soul does not leave the body, nor is it joined with it in a total union, except through the change of each from its own power and property, and after the conversion of their natures. This is the "dissolution and congealing" which the philosophers spoke of previously. ...so that it might be removed from common understanding. And let this be an example of the veiled and obscure speech of the philosophers used among them: *Anoint the leaf with poison* <note>original: "toxico"; in alchemy, "poison" often refers to a transformative or corrosive agent like mercury or arsenic</note>, and the beginning of the office, or rather the mastery of the same, will be proven to you. And they say: *Work the strong bodies with dissolved law* <note>original: "iure soluto"; likely referring to a chemical solvent or "acid"</note>, until both of them are converted to their own subtlety. Similarly, the saying of the wise man among them is: *Unless you convert the bodies into subtlety, so that they are fine and impalpable to the touch, that which you seek will not be directed to you.* And if they have not been ground down, return to the work until they are ground and become subtle; for if you do this, what you desire will be directed to you.

And in this manner, they set down many such words about these things. Nor could any of those testing the art reach this hidden fact of such concealment in any way, until a good opening of the shown doctrine appeared to him, removing the preceding doubt. And similarly, they named the "composition" after the "solution" and "congealing." Afterward, they also said that the composition is not completed except with "marriage" <note>the chemical union of substances</note> and "putrefaction" <note>the breaking down or fermentation of matter</note>. And again, their later speech taught concerning solution, congealing, and division, and concerning marriage, putrefaction, and composition.

### On Decoction and its Effect. Chapter 4.

And you should know that the philosophers have named "decoction" <note>original: "decoctio"; a process of heating or boiling a substance in a liquid to extract its essence or change its state</note> in their books. ### On the fixation of the spirit. Chapter VI.

And know that when the body mixes itself with moisture, and the heat of the fire finds it, the moisture is turned upon the body and dissolves it; and then the spirit cannot depart from it, because it has soaked itself in with the fire. And spirits are fleeting <note>volatile</note> until the bodies are mixed with them and attempt to fight against the fire and its flame. And yet these parts agree but little, except through good operation and continuous and long labor, because the nature of the soul is to tend upward, where the center of the soul is. And who among the experimenters is able to join two or diverse things whose centers are different, except after the conversion of their natures, and the mutation of the substance and the thing from its own nature—which is a difficult thing to seek. Therefore, he who is able to convert the soul into the body, and the body into the soul, and to mix the subtle spirits with it, shall tinge <note>transform or dye</note> every body.

## *On the separation of the elements of the stone.* Chapter IX.

Then it is necessary, O brother—whom may God honor—that you take the honored or precious stone which the wise have named, magnified, hidden, and concealed. And place it in a gourd-shaped vessel <term>cucurbita: a glass vessel used in distillation, named for its gourd-like shape</term> with its still-head <term>alembic: the cap or apparatus used to condense and direct vapors during distillation</term>, and separate its natures; that is, the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire. And these are the body and soul, the spirit and the tincture. 

And when you have separated the water from the earth, and the air from the fire, keep each of the two by itself. Take that which descends to the bottom of the vessel, which is the dross <note>original: "fex"; the solid residue or "lees" remaining after distillation</note>, and wash it with hot fire until its blackness is taken away and its thickness departs. Whiten it with a good whitening, and make the additions of moisture fly away from it; then it will be converted and become a white lime <note>original: "calx"; a powder produced by heating a substance to high temperatures</note>, in which there shall be no dark obscurity, nor impurity, nor opposition. 

Afterward, return to the first natures which ascended from it, and cleanse them likewise from impurity, blackness, and opposition; repeat the process upon them many times until they are refined, purified, and thinned. And when you have done this, God has already had mercy on you. 

And know, brother, that this work is one stone, upon which no "Garib" <note>original: "Garib"; a Latinization of the Arabic 'gharib', meaning a stranger or foreign substance</note>—that is, anything else—may enter. With this the wise operate, and from it comes that with which it is medicated until it is completed. Nothing is mixed with it, neither in part nor in the whole. And this stone is found at all times, and in every place, and with every person; the finding of it does not burden the seeker, wherever they may be. And it is a vile stone, black and stinking; it is not bought for a price, and without anything else, it is not light in weight. They call it the *Origin of the World* <note>original: "Origo mundi"</note> because it rises up like things that are germinating. And this is its revelation and appearance to the seeker.

### *On the nature of the Stone and its origin. Chapter 10.*

# THE EMERALD
## TABLET OF HERMES

->*Trismegistus <note>Thrice-Greatest</note>. On Alchemy <note>original Greek: Περὶ χυμείας</note>. By an uncertain translator.*<-

<image-desc>The main text begins with a large decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring ornate foliate designs and scrolls within a square frame.</image-desc>

The Words of the Secrets of Hermes, which were written upon the Emerald Tablet, found between his hands in a dark cave in which his buried body was discovered. It is true, without falsehood, certain, and most true. That which is below is like that which is above. And that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of the one thing. And just as all things were from one, by the mediation of the one, so all things were born from this one thing by adaptation. Its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon. The wind carried it in its belly. Its nurse is the earth. The father of all the perfection <note>original: telesmi, referring to the "telesma" or the completed work of alchemy</note> of the whole world is here. Its power is complete if it be turned into earth. You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently and with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth to the heaven, and again it descends to the earth, and receives the power of the higher and the lower things. So shall you have the glory of the whole world. Therefore all obscurity shall flee from you. This is the strong fortitude of all fortitude, because it will overcome every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing. Thus was the world created. From this shall come wonderful adaptations, the method of which is this. Therefore I am called Hermes Trismegistus, having three parts of the philosophy of the whole world. That which I have said concerning the operation of the Sun is completed.

# THE GARDENER PHILOSOPHER
### From the Maritime Gardens; A Brief Commentary on the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "περὶ χυμείας" (peri chymeias)</note> concerning Alchemy. <term>Alchemy: the ancient art of transformation, seeking to perfect both metals and the human spirit.</term>

->The Prayer of the Gardener.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring scrolling vine and floral patterns.</image-desc>PRAISE, honor, power, and glory be unto thee, Lord God Almighty, with thy beloved son our Lord Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit the Comforter. O Holy Trinity, who art the only and one God, and perfect man, I give thanks to thee. Because, when I had come to know the transitory things of this world and its adversaries, thou didst lift me out of the same by thy supreme mercy, lest I be provoked by its delights. But because I see infinite numbers of people deceived in this art, who do not enter upon the direct path, may it please thee, my Lord God, that from the knowledge which thou hast delivered to me, I may turn my dear friends away from this error; so that when they have perceived the truth, they may praise thy holy and glorious name, which is blessed forever, Amen.

->P R E F A C E.<-

I, called the Gardener <note>original: "Hortulanus"</note>, so named from the maritime gardens, wrapped in a Jacobine skin <note>likely referring to the habit of a Dominican friar, often called Jacobins</note>, and unworthy to be called a disciple of philosophy. Moved by the love of my dear friend, I intend to provide the most certain explanation of the Speech of Hermes, the father of philosophers. Which speech, although it be hidden, nevertheless the exercise of the true work through the labor of my own fingers has most truly revealed the entire exposition. For the concealment used by philosophers in their writings profits nothing where the teaching of the Holy Spirit is at work.

# THE GARDENER

### That the art of Alchemy is true and certain. Chapter 1.

The philosopher says: **IT IS TRUE**, namely, that the art of Alchemy has been given to us. **WITHOUT A LIE**. He says this to express his loathing for those who claim the art is a lie, that is, false. **CERTAIN**, meaning it has been proven by experience. For whatever is proven by experience is most certain, **AND MOST TRUE**. Because the truest Sun <note>original: "Sol"; in alchemy, this refers to gold</note> is brought forth through the art. And he says "most true" in the superlative degree, because the Sun generated through this art exceeds all natural Sun <note>natural gold</note> in all medicinal properties and others.

### That the stone must be divided into two parts. Chapter 2.

Consequently, he touches upon the operation of the stone, saying: **THAT WHICH IS BELOW IS LIKE THAT WHICH IS ABOVE**. And he says this for this reason: That this stone is divided into two principal parts through the mastery <note>original: "magisterium"; the technical process of the alchemical work</note>. Into an upper part, which ascends above, and into a lower part, which remains below, fixed and clear. And yet these two parts agree in virtue. And therefore he says: **THAT WHICH IS ABOVE IS LIKE THAT WHICH IS BELOW**. Moreover, that division is necessary **TO ACCOMPLISH THE MIRACLES OF ONE THING**, namely, the stone. Because the lower part is the earth, which is called the Nurse and the ferment. And the upper part is the soul, which quickens and resurrects the whole stone; and therefore, once the separation is made and the union celebrated, many miracles are accomplished in the secret work of nature.

### That the stone has within itself the four elements. Chapter 3.

**AND JUST AS ALL THINGS WERE FROM ONE BY THE MEDITATION OF ONE.** Here he gives an example, saying:

<keywords>Alchemy, Gold, Emerald Tablet, Mastery, Ferment, Soul and Body, Elements, Hermeticism</keywords>

# COMMENTARY

Just as all things came from one—namely, from a confused globe or a confused mass—by the meditation (that is, the thought and creation) of the One (that is, Almighty God), **SO ALL THINGS WERE BORN** (that is, they emerged) **FROM THIS ONE THING**, meaning from that one confused mass. **BY ADAPTATION**, that is, by the sole command and miracle of God. In the same way, our Stone <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the legendary substance believed to be capable of turning base metals into gold and providing an elixir of life.</note> is born and has emerged from one confused mass containing all elements within itself, which was created by God; and by His miracle alone, our Stone is born from it.

### *That the Stone has a father and a mother, namely the Sun and the Moon. Chapter 4.*

And just as we see that in nature one animal generates more animals similar to itself, so in our art the Sun generates the Sun by the power of the multiplication of the aforementioned Stone. Therefore it follows: **ITS FATHER IS THE SUN**, meaning the "gold of the philosophers" <note>original: "aurum philosophorum"; this refers not to common gold, but to a refined spiritual or chemical principle.</note>. And because in every natural generation there must be a suitable and convenient receptacle, possessing a certain harmony of likeness to the father, so also in this artificial generation it is necessary that the Sun has a suitable receptacle for its seed and its tincture <term>tincture: a potent substance or "spirit" capable of transmuting and coloring base matter</term> that is harmonious with it; and this is the "silver of the philosophers." And therefore it follows: **ITS MOTHER IS THE MOON.**

### *That the joining of the parts of the Stone is called impregnation. Chapter 5.*

When these two have received one another in the joining of the Stone, the Stone is impregnated in the belly of the wind; and this is what is said afterward: **THE WIND CARRIED IT IN ITS BELLY.** It is clear that the wind is air, and air is life, and life is the soul. I have already spoken above concerning the soul, which gives life to the whole Stone. And thus it is necessary that the wind carries and brings back the whole Stone, and brings forth the Mastery <term>magisterium: the completed work or the "Great Work" of alchemy</term>. And then it follows that it receives nourishment from its nurse, which is the earth.

<summary>This page provides an alchemical commentary on the Emerald Tablet, explaining how the Philosopher's Stone originates from a divine "confused mass" and is generated through the symbolic union of the Sun (gold) and Moon (silver).</summary>
<keywords>Philosopher's Stone, Sun and Moon, Alchemy, Creation, Gold of the Philosophers, Silver of the Philosophers, Impregnation, Magisterium, Elements</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Emerald Tablet, specifically focusing on the roles of the "Nurse" and the "Earth" in the alchemical process. It follows the previous discussion regarding the "Wind" carrying the stone in its belly.</meta>

->THE GARDENER<-

And therefore the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Emerald Tablet</note> says: THE EARTH IS ITS NURSE. Because just as an infant would never reach maturity without the nourishment of a nurse, so our Stone <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the alchemical Great Work</note> would never reach its effect without the fermentation of its earth. This fermentation is indeed called nourishment. For in this way, it is generated from one father with the union of the mother. The things—that is, the sons—are like the father; yet if they lack long decoction <note>A process of heating or boiling a substance in a liquid</note>, they will be like the mother in whiteness, and will retain the weight of the father.

### *That the Stone is perfect if the soul is fixed in the body. Chapter VI.*

Afterward follows: THE FATHER OF ALL THE TELESMI OF THE WHOLE WORLD IS HERE. This means that in the work of the Stone is the final path. And take note: the Philosopher calls the operation the "father of every *telesmus*" <note>original: "telesmi"; a Greek-derived term meaning a "perfection," "completion," or "consecrated object," often interpreted by alchemists as a secret or treasure</note>, that is, of every secret or every treasure of the whole world—meaning every Stone found in this world. "Is here"—as if he were to say, "Behold, I show it to you." Afterward the Philosopher says: Do you wish for me to teach you when the strength of the Stone is perfect and complete? Namely, when it has been turned into its own earth. And therefore he says: ITS POWER IS INTEGRAL—that is, perfect and complete—IF IT BE TURNED INTO EARTH. This means if the soul of the Stone itself, which was mentioned above (for the soul is called "wind" and "air," in which is the whole life and strength of the Stone), should be converted into the earth (namely, the earth of the Stone) and be fixed, so that the entire substance of the Stone is so joined with its nurse (namely, the earth), that the whole Stone is turned into ferment. Just as in the making of bread, a little leaven <note>original: "fermentum"</note> nourishes and ferments a great quantity of dough, and thus converts the whole substance of the dough into leaven; so the Philosopher intends that our Stone be so fermented that it acts as a leaven for the multiplication of the Stone.

<summary>This page explains the alchemical metaphor of the "Earth" as a nurse that feeds the Stone, emphasizing that the "soul" (volatile air) must be fixed into the "body" (solid earth) to achieve perfection. It likens the multiplication of the Philosopher's Stone to the way yeast leavens a large batch of dough.</summary>

### On the purification of the stone. Chapter VII.

</margin>
Consequently, he sets forth how it ought to be multiplied. But first, he describes the purification of the stone and the separation of its parts, saying: YOU SHALL SEPARATE THE EARTH FROM THE FIRE, THE SUBTLE FROM THE GROSS, GENTLY WITH GREAT INGENUITY. Gently, that is, little by little, not through violence, but with ingenuity—namely, in the philosophical manure <note>original: "fimo philosophico"; a term for a gentle, steady heat source like a dung-bed or water bath</note>. You shall separate, that is, you shall dissolve. For dissolution is the separation of parts. The earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross. That is, the dregs and impurities from the fire, air, and water, and from the entire substance of the stone, so that the stone remains there most pure, without any filth.

### *That the non-fixed part of the stone ought to overcome the*
### *fixed part, and elevate it. Chapter VIII.*

And the stone thus prepared is fit for multiplication. And now he describes its multiplication and its easy liquefaction into a power of penetration <note>original: "uirtute ingressibili"; the ability of the alchemical medicine to penetrate and transform solid metals</note>, as much in hard bodies as in soft, saying: IT ASCENDS FROM THE EARTH INTO HEAVEN, AND AGAIN IT DESCENDS INTO THE EARTH. Here it is greatly to be noted, that although our stone in the first operation is divided into four parts, which are the four elements, nevertheless, as was said above, two of its parts are primary. One which ascends above, which is called "non-fixed," and another which remains below "fixed," which is called earth, or the ferment, which nourishes and ferments the whole stone, as has been said. Of that non-fixed part, it is necessary to have a great quantity and to give it to the stone—which has been made most pure without filth—so many times through the mastery <note>original: "magisterium"; the technical process or "Great Work" of the alchemist</note>, until the whole stone, by the power of the spirit...

### Chapter IX. How the volatile stone must be fixed again.

Afterward, this same stone, having been thus exalted, must be softened with the oil extracted from the stone itself during the first operation—which is called the "water of the stone"—and roasted so many times by sublimating, until by the power of the fermentation of the earth exalted with it, the entire stone may once again descend from heaven to earth, and remain fixed and flowing. And this is what the philosopher says: IT DESCENDS AGAIN TO THE EARTH, AND SO IT RECEIVES THE FORCE OF THE HIGHER THINGS by sublimating, AND OF THE LOWER THINGS by descending; that is to say, that which is bodily shall become spiritual by sublimating, and that which is spiritual shall become bodily by descending.

### Chapter X. On the fruit of the art, and the efficacy of the stone.

THUS YOU SHALL HAVE THE GLORY OF THE WHOLE WORLD; that is, with this stone so composed, you shall possess the glory of this world. THEREFORE ALL OBSCURITY SHALL FLEE FROM YOU. That is, all poverty and sickness. Because the stone made in this way is a healer of every infirmity. THIS IS THE STRONG FORTITUDE OF ALL FORTITUDE. Because there is no comparison of other strengths of this world to the strength of this stone. BECAUSE IT WILL CONQUER EVERY SUBTLE THING, AND WILL PENETRATE EVERY SOLID THING. It will conquer—that is, by conquering it will convert "living mercury" <note>original: "Mercurium uiuum"; likely referring to quicksilver or the philosophical principle of fluidity</note> by congealing it, which is subtle; and it will penetrate other hard, solid, and firm bodies.

# COMMENTARY

Next, the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or the commentator</note> provides an example regarding the **Composition of his stone**, saying: SO THE WORLD WAS CREATED. This means that just as the world was created, so too is our stone made. For in the beginning, the entire world and everything within it was one confused mass, or a confused chaos, as was stated above. Afterward, through the craftsmanship of the supreme Creator, that mass was divided into the four elements, marvelously separated and rectified; because of this separation, diverse things are brought forth. In the same way, diverse things can be produced through the adaptation of our work, by the separation of different elements from different bodies. HENCE WILL BE MARVELOUS ADAPTATIONS. That is, if you separate the elements, marvelous compounds will be made, suitable for our work in the composition of our stone, through the joining of the rectified elements. OF WHICH—that is, concerning these marvels suited to this purpose—THE METHOD—namely, of operating—IS GIVEN HERE.

->*An enigmatic suggestion regarding what constitutes the matter of the stone. Chapter XII.*<-

And so I AM CALLED HERMES TRISMEGISTUS <note>original: "Hermes Trismegistus," meaning "Thrice-Greatest Hermes," a legendary figure credited with the founding of alchemy.</note>. He names himself first so that his disciples who arrive at this knowledge might perpetually remember his name. Then he touches upon what it consists of, saying: HAVING THREE PARTS OF THE PHILOSOPHY OF THE WHOLE WORLD. Because whatever is in the world having matter and form is composed of the four elements. Thus, there are infinite parts of the world, all of which the philosopher divides into three principal parts: namely, the Mineral, the Vegetable, and the Animal parts, concerning which...

<header>THE GARDENER'S COMMENTARY</header> <note>original: "HORTVLANI COMMENT." Hortulanus is a pseudonym for an alchemist, likely meaning "The Gardener."</note>

jointly or separately, the philosopher possessed true knowledge in the work of the Sun <note>The "Work of the Sun" refers to the creation of gold or the final stage of the alchemical process.</note>. And for this reason he says, "having the three parts of the philosophy of the whole world," which parts are contained within a single stone, namely, the Mercury of the Philosophers <term>Mercury of the Philosophers: not common quicksilver, but the essential "soul" or "spirit" of matter sought by alchemists</term>.

### *Why the stone is called perfect. Chapter XIII.*

And for this reason, this stone is called "perfect," because it possesses within itself the nature of minerals, vegetables, and animals. For it is a stone triple and one, having four natures—namely the four elements—and three colors: namely black, white, and red. It is also called a "grain of wheat," which, unless it dies, remains alone; but if it dies (as was said above), when it is joined in union, it brings forth much fruit—namely, when the aforementioned operations are completed. O dear reader, if you understand the operation of the stone, I have told you the truth; and if you do not understand, I have told you nothing. WHAT I HAVE SAID CONCERNING THE OPERATION OF THE SUN IS COMPLETED; that is, what was said concerning the operation of the stone is finished, consisting of three colors and four natures existing, as was said, in a single thing: namely, in the philosophical Mercury alone.

->T H E  E N D.<-

->by Matthias Apiarius, at the cost and expense<-
->of the honorable man, Johann Petreius, Printer of Nuremberg.<-
->In the year 1545,<-
->In the month of August.<-

# JOHANNES PETREIUS, PRINTER,
## SENDS GREETINGS TO THE STUDIOUS READER.

You have before you at present, studious reader, a few—but by no means common—short works on <term>chrysopoeia</term> <note>original: "χρυσοποιΐα"; the art of making gold</note>. If I perceive that these have been pleasing to you, I shall shortly bring to light more and even better works of this kind from among those I have in my possession. However, since the manuscript copies are partly corrupted by age and neglect, and partly distorted by the ignorance of scribes—so much so that they cannot be corrected and improved without the comparison of many copies—I ask that if anyone possesses any of these, whether in Latin or in German, they would be willing to generously share them with me. Thus, by comparing many copies, more accurate versions may reach the hands of students. Whoever does this will earn no small favor among the candidates of this art, and will receive from me several printed copies, along with their own original manuscript untouched, as a gift. These, moreover, are the works we have in our possession; we have marked the best of them with an asterisk.

* Seven Treatises of Hermes Trismegistus.
* The Dialogue of Mary the Prophetess.
* The Assembly of the Philosophers <note>original: "Turba philosophorum"; one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>.
* Morienus.
The Book of Distinctions.
* Alphidius. Avicenna on Minerals.
The Light of Lights.
* Lambardus the Philosopher.
* The Lily of Intelligence.
The Book of Saturn.
Another book by Roger Bacon addressed to a certain Cardinal.
The Mirror of Alchemy by Brother Elias of the Order of Friars Minor.
The same author's Letter from the Sun to the Moon.
* The Palm-branch of Theosophy.
The Rose Garden of Arnold of Villanova.
Questions by the same author.
The Old Testament by the same author.

<column-break/>

The New Testament by the same author.
The Lily by Master Blasius of Parma.
Another Lily by an uncertain author.
* The New Pearl <note>original: "Margarita nouella"; likely the "Precious New Pearl" by Petrus Bonus</note>.
The Book of Roots.
The Golden Rose.
Johannes de Rupescissa.
* Dialogue on the Little Golden Book.
Petrus de Zeleuco.
The Practice of the Philosophers.
Duns Scotus the Subtle.
Thomas Aquinas to Brother Reginald.
Johannes Tecenensis.
The Sayings of Alanus.
The Book of the Trinity.
The Mirror of the Elements by Johannes of Vienna.
* Many works of Raymond Lull, whom we especially desire to provide in his entirety.

->THE END.<-

Such emblems were essential in the early printing era, acting as a trademark to guarantee the quality and authenticity of the scholarly works produced by a specific press. The bear is a play on the name of his family's printing tradition in Nuremberg.</note>

# DESCRIPTION OF THE BINDING

<note>The binding of this volume is heavily worn and stained. The decorative patterns were created using "blind-tooling," a technique where heated metal stamps are pressed into the leather without the application of gold leaf or ink, resulting in a subtle, recessed design.</note>

This volume is encased in a **blind-tooled** pigskin or vellum binding, likely dating to the 16th or 17th century. The decorative scheme consists of several concentric rectangular borders created with **roll-stamps** <note>a cylindrical metal tool engraved with a pattern, used to roll a continuous design onto the leather</note>.

### THE DECORATIVE BORDERS

The outer vertical and horizontal bands feature a series of allegorical or biblical figures standing in small niches. While much of the detail has been lost to time and surface dirt, one figure in the right-hand vertical band remains identifiable by a label:

->**PRUDENCE**<-
<note>original: "PRVDEN," an abbreviation for the Latin *Prudentia*. In Renaissance art, the virtue of Prudence is often depicted as a woman holding a mirror or a serpent, representing self-knowledge and wisdom.</note>

The inner frames contain more delicate patterns of flowers and foliage. In the very center of the cover—the central rectangular field—there is a vertical row of four large, stylized ornaments shaped like flowers or pomegranates.

### CONDITION AND HARDWARE

The binding shows the passage of centuries:
*   The leather is significantly darkened and stained.
*   The surface is worn, making much of the stamped text and imagery illegible.
*   On the left edge, the remnants of two **metal clasps** are visible; these would have once held the heavy volume tightly shut to prevent the parchment or paper from warping.

<summary>This page provides a physical description of the book's 16th-century blind-tooled leather binding, highlighting its allegorical decorations and signs of historical wear. It identifies the personification of Prudence as one of the few remaining legible figures in the decorative border.</summary>
